Piers taught me the wheel, so I can build it properly now. The Hall is damaged and Alys will repair it. Please keep sending whoever owes us days to the Mill House wheel.
Rain's on. I'm asking Piers for a session on the water mill, since that's the wheel I owe the Arderns. I'll gather firewood after.
Mary, Rob, Joan: the Arderns want your owed days on the Mill House wheel today, with Piers.
Hugh, Odo: the Hearnes are nearly out of grain, with barley 2-3 days off. I'll work for you for 10 grain, or repay a loan from our harvest. Tell me what work you want.
Will, you take the bed tonight, dry as you can get. I'll lie on the floor by the hearth. Tell me if you're still hungry and I'll share my bread tomorrow.

Fog today, so I'm gathering firewood at the Coppice for the Hall. Mary, Rob, Joan, Tom and Kit still owe their days on the Mill House wheel. I'll send them when the fog lifts. I'm leaving Wat's timber offer to you.
I'm at the Mill House too, working the owed day. I'll ask Piers to teach us both. I'll keep a unit back tonight.
Tomorrow I'll go to the Mill House early to work the owed day with Piers.
Will, eat your share cooked at the hearth before anything else, and don't go out in the wet tomorrow unless you must.

Morning. We'll both go to the Mill House now and work the Arderns' owed day on the wheel with Piers, then ask him to teach us. Tonight we sleep at the camp; if we have a unit left over, we'll try for a child.
Piers: Rob and I are here to work the Arderns' owed day on the wheel. Will you teach us both while we work?

We sleep at the camp tonight. In the morning let's go to the Mill House together first, work my owed day on the wheel for the Arderns, and ask Piers to teach us both. I'll keep my units for the wheel.
Tom, I'll weed the Long Field today for the Hearnes. I'm still owed a day on the Arderns' wheel (A227), and I'll work it once the reaping is done.
Thank you, Kit. I'll eat my share cooked before anything else, and I'll stay dry tomorrow unless the reaping needs me.
Hugh, Odo: the barley must be cut tomorrow or it is lost. I'll reap all day. Can the wheel spare you?
I've hired Tom for 3 days (O217) for 10 grain. Send him and every hand that owes us a day to the wheel at the Mill House.
Wat took the Hall repair and Piers is on 5 more days. Odo, is the Hall sound now? Tomorrow send Tom (3 days, A336) and everyone else who owes us a day to the wheel.

Alys, reap, yes. The Hearnes' bins are low, and the village can't lose that crop. Ask them for a share of grain for your day. I'll keep on the wheel with Piers and Tom. Odo, no need to learn walling: Wat took our 8 grain for 2 days and worked at the Hall today. Just check it's sound once he's done.

I reaped 6.2 grain today and it is in the Hearne store. Tomorrow I'll go back to the Long Field and reap what is still standing, using all my units. Will, keep the bed and eat your cooked share first.
Let's go to the Mill House together this morning. I'll work my owed day for the Arderns on the wheel, and I'll ask Piers again whether he'll teach us.
We sleep at the camp tonight. Tomorrow I'll ask Piers what the wheel needs and work my owed day on it, and we'll ask him to teach us both.

Well done, Joan, 31 grain! The Long Field is the Hearnes', though. Ask Ellen tomorrow what share is fair, and give them their part, so nobody calls it theft. Reaping for a share keeps us in their good books.

Hugh: I've reaped 12 grain for us over two days. The Hearnes haven't named a share yet, so I'll ask them. I don't know about Wat's wall. Odo can check it. Tomorrow I'll reap again if any barley is left, then go to the wheel.

Good: help Alys get the barley in today before it's lost, then come to the wheel if you can. Wat holds A332 (2 days on the Hall), so leave the stone to him. Send Tom and every hand that owes us a day to the Mill House.

The wheel is down to about 100 units of work. Alys, Odo: did the barley all come in, and did the Hearnes give us a share? Did Wat finish the wall today? Tomorrow, send every hand who owes us a day to the Mill House.

The wheel is down to about 100 units of work. Alys, Odo: did the barley all come in, and did the Hearnes give us a share? Did Wat finish the wall today? Tomorrow, send every hand who owes us a day to the Mill House.

Wat, the Hearnes' hut was full, so my 8 grain lies at their door; I'll tell Ellen. I reaped 6.5 grain more. Tomorrow I'll bring in the grain at our door if the cellar has room, and tell Ellen about their share.
Good, Wat, thank you for returning it. I'll leave the grain at the door until the cellar is done, then carry it in. I'll also speak to Ellen about the Hearnes' share.
Let's go to the Mill House together, I'll work my owed day for the Arderns on the wheel, and we'll ask Piers to teach us both.
Go to the Mill House and work your day, but take it gently. Ask Piers to teach us. I'm reaping the Long Field and giving the Hearnes their share.
We have grain enough now. Tomorrow I'll go to the Mill House to work my owed day for the Arderns. Rest well, Mary.
Good, Joan. The cellar will be done by midday tomorrow, and after that our grain at the door can all come in. Tell Ellen that what lies at their door is their share, and the 2.4 I left there too.
The Long Field is cleared, nothing left to reap. I've barred the door tonight because the store has been picked at. Tomorrow I'll bake bread and settle my day owed to the Arderns.

The barley is in. Today, please send Tom (A336, 3 days) and Mary, Rob and Joan (they each owe a day) to the wheel at the Mill House, and come yourself if you can. Also check whether Wat has made the Hall wall sound.

The wheel is down to about 93 units, but only Piers and I are on it. Tom took 6 of our timber for 12 grain. Odo, is the Hall wall sound now? Tomorrow, could one of you come to the wheel, and call on Mary, Rob, Joan and Tom for the days they owe us?

I took firewood from the heaps at the Green today, not knowing whose they were. I have it still and will give it back or account for it to whoever holds it. Tomorrow I'll work my owed day for the Arderns.
Hugh: the Hall looks sound to me; Wat has put fresh timber in its walls. Tomorrow I'll go to the Mill House wheel myself and ask Mary, Rob, Joan and Tom to come for the days they owe us.

The barley is in, and the Hall is mended, so thank you, Wat. Mary, Rob, Joan, Tom and the Hearnes: you owe days on the mill wheel. Please come to the Mill House today or tomorrow. Once it turns, everyone gets flour instead of hand meal.
Hugh, I owe the Arderns days and will pay them, but my time is very near and I cannot go to the Mill House until the child is born. I'll come after, or pay in hay or firewood.
Tom, I'll fell timber in the Coppice for the granary today. The Arderns' wheel debt (A227) waits until the timber is in.
Mary, Rob, Joan and Tom: you each owe the Arderns a day on the mill wheel. Come now and work your days off.
Thank you. I'll rest at the Hall today. Please teach me the wheel craft when you can.
Hugh, Odo: my time is near, so I'll stay near the Hall and not walk far. Hugh, please ask the Hearnes and the others for grain in place of the days they owe. Tomorrow I'll help where I can.

Don't set time aside to learn from me: my teach was refused today because I don't know the wheel well enough yet. Piers could teach you, but his days are paid for the wheel. Tomorrow, please ask Mary, Rob, Tom and the Hearnes for grain instead of the days they owe (about 3 grain a day), then gather firewood or cut hay. Alys: rest near the Hall.
Mary, you owe the Arderns a day on the wheel. Can you pay in grain or firewood instead? Tell Hugh what you will give. Hugh, the Mill Mead forage is nearly bare, so I found only 0.2 wild food.

The wheel is at about 72 units. Mary, you're welcome by the fire tonight. Odo, what did the debtors say they'd pay? Mary, Rob still owes his wheel day: grain or firewood to the Hall store will settle it.
Thank you, Mary. A123 is paid and released. Alys, don't wear yourself out foraging bare ground; rest. Odo, the same deal goes for the others: 3 grain and 2 firewood for each day owed.

Mary, Rob, Tom, the Hearnes and Joan: the wheel is now Piers and Hugh's alone, so Hugh asks you to pay what you owe the Arderns in grain or firewood, taken to the Ardern Hall store, instead of days. Tell me what you'll bring.
Mary: you owe the Arderns a day on the wheel (A123). Hugh asks grain or firewood instead. What will you bring to the Ardern Hall store, and when?
Yes, ask Wright about their house. I'm paying the Arderns 4 grain for our debt, so you needn't go to the wheel. Stay with Godwin.
Odo, I'm bringing 10 grain to the Ardern Hall store now toward the Hearne debts, and more later.

Rob, Joan, Tom, Ellen: thank you. A128, A181, A222 and A227 are released as paid. Wat: A332 was already released. I choose 4 coin for the Hall oven; tell me when you start and I'll pay. Piers: 6 firewood from the Hall is yours, as a gift for the wheel.
Wat, I minded Agnes and brought in 4 firewood from the Green heap, which may not be ours. I'll ask whose it is tomorrow and pay it back if anyone claims it.
Yes, Wat: 4 firewood is in our store, taken from the Green heap, which isn't surely ours. I'll find out whose it is and repay. Glad the wheel debt is clear.

Debts so far: Rob's A128 is paid (4 grain). Joan has paid 4 grain and 1.9 firewood, Tom 10 grain, Ellen 5 grain, all into the Hall store. Mary's A123 is released. Rate: 3 grain and 2 firewood per day owed. Rob's A128 and Joan's A181 and A299 are still open, as are Tom's A222 and A336 and the Hearnes' A227. Piers' A505 is five days. I'm cutting firewood on Gorse Bank today for the Hall store, since
A222 is counted paid. I've left 20 grain at the Hall in all, so more may be owed. Tomorrow: firewood and timber, and bring the door grain into the new store. Keep the door barred.

Joan, Hugh has counted your wheel debt as paid. Well done. We now have the 20 stone for his oven. Tomorrow I'll settle the price with him and start building. Did you find any firewood? Our fuel is nearly gone.
Following your word: I'm felling timber in the Coppice with the crude tool today and will bring it to the Hall store. The 0.9 firewood goes in now.

[Plans] Winter day 1: I accepted O590 (4 coin for work 4 days), which is Hugh's oven deal. The oven needs 20 stone, 2 timber and 12 units at the Ardern Hall. I carried the stone up and started. I gave Joan my crude tool. Joan goes to Holm Wood at nightfall, and I mind Agnes (work care) while she's away. Fuel is critical; the store's 2 timber covers about 1 cold night. Make myself another crude tool later.

[Mill wheel] The Arderns' Mill House has a water wheel and leat begun, materials in, about 150 units left. I'm the only one who can build it. Get the pay agreed before working. Day 1 of summer: offered it to everyone, and put up a standing offer of 5 days' work for 15 grain.

[Debts] A23 and A327 are settled. A505: 5 days on the wheel for the Arderns, 15 grain already received. Days 1-3 were autumn days 6-8. Day 4 is winter day 1 and day 5 is winter day 2, then Hugh releases it. Next: another 5 days for 15 grain (Hugh agreed). About 53 units were left on the wheel at the start of winter. Fuel: 7 firewood and 7 timber at the start of winter, about 4 cold nights. I asked Hugh fo
Good, put your day to the wheel and I'll work beside you. Ask Piers what he knows of wheels. If he'll lend a hand, I'll pay him 5 coin a day, the same as my standing offer.

The leat clearing would not take at Mill Garth, so your day is still owed under A25. Tomorrow I will go to Mill Garth and talk to Piers about the wheel for the household, and put my day to the wheel for you.
Odo, I'm at the wheel all day. Your owed day under A25 goes there too, and Piers can show us how it goes. If the work won't take, cut hay on Mill Mead instead.

The wheel wouldn't take my hands today, so I cut hay instead. It's in the store now. Piers knows the wheel and we don't, so let's keep him at it and pay him well. Joan and Tom each owe me a day for my coin. Odo, do you know of work they could do to help the mill, like carrying timber or clearing the garth? Alys, did your work on the wheel take today?

Ask Piers this morning what carrying or clearing the wheel needs. If he names something, set Joan and Tom to it for their owed days. Ask him too whether he'll teach one of us the wheel; I'd pay coin for it.
Piers, Hugh asks what the wheel needs carried or cleared, so Joan and Tom can be set to it for their owed days. Will you also teach one of us the wheel? Hugh will pay coin for it.

Good, Joan. You gave him a full day of hay, so that should settle the work. Ask Hugh straight out whether the debt is paid. Asking Piers about timber is right. Tell him I'll trade stone or a day of mason's work for it.

The Hall is cracking and I can't mend stone; it's a mason's work. Tomorrow I'll offer Wat grain or coin to repair it before it gets worse. I cut about 19 hay today and took 4 more timber to the Mill House, so there are 9 there now for Piers. Odo, does Piers still owe us his days on A17? I'd like the wheel kept going every day.

Agreed, Wat. First thing tomorrow I'll find Hugh. I'll ask whether his day of work is settled and whether we may fell in the Coppice in return for a hearth. Then I'll go to Piers and offer stone or a hearth for 4 timber.
Piers, Hugh asks what the wheel needs carried or cleared, so Joan and Tom can be set to it for their owed days. Will you teach one of us the wheel for the coin Hugh offered?
Piers: what does the water wheel need carried or cleared? Hugh wants Joan and Tom set to it for their owed days. And will you teach one of us the wheel? Hugh will pay coin.

The Masons' roof fell in last night. Hugh, I'm felling a few poles in your Coppice to mend it, and I'll repay the lord in mason's work. Piers or anyone else: I'll give coin or a day of mason's work for timber. See my offers.
Joan, I'm mending the roof today. Settle Hugh's debt if you can, then gather firewood or forage for us. I've offered Piers stone and grain for timber.

Joan, the roof is down and nobody would sell me timber today. Tomorrow I'll fell timber in the Coppice with the crude tools, if Hugh will allow it. Will you find Hugh first and ask if his day of work is settled, and if he'll let us fell in the Coppice in return for a hearth at the Mill House? Then find Piers: I'll trade stone or a hearth for 4 timber. We need about 6 timber to repair the roof.

Wat owes us a day of mason's work (A318) for 4 timber. Tomorrow I'll ask him to mend the Hall wall. Odo, may I borrow your crude tool for the hay? Bare-handed I got only 1 hay today. Alys, shall we try for a child tonight?
I've asked Hugh aloud for leave to fell in the Coppice for repayment in mason's work. I'm felling now with a crude tool and will bring the timber to the cottage store.
Hugh: may the Masons fell a few poles in the Coppice? Wat will repay you with mason's work or a hearth. I'm felling for our roof now unless you say no.

Hugh, the wheel's materials are all in, so nothing more needs carrying. I worked it on day 6 and I'm on it again today. That's 4 grain owed under A17 (2 for day 6, 2 for today). Please leave it in Wright's House store. My roof leaks, so I'll mend it first this morning.
Joan, I'm using your 2.3 timber to start mending the roof. Please ask Hugh whether we may fell in the Coppice in return for a hearth at the Mill House. If he says no, tell me before I cut.

Joan, the roof is mended and the cottage is sound again. Hugh took my offer of a day's work for 4 timber, so I owe him a day. Did he say what he wants done? I'd guess a hearth at the Mill House. You've got plenty of timber and hay: keep the timber for an upgrade to a timber house. I've put firewood in the store for tonight.

Well done, Joan. The roof is already mended, so that timber can go towards rebuilding the cottage in timber. That takes 6 timber, and with mine we have 9. But make sure Hugh agrees to the felling first. We owe him a day of my work for 4 timber, so offer the felling as part of that bargain.
Father, I'm working for Hugh this morning at the Mill House, clearing the leat, to pay off what I owe him. I'll come to the Long Field after.

Wat: you owe us a day for the 4 timber (A318). Please spend it today mending the Ardern Hall's cracked wall and roof. Joan: yes, take a few poles from the Coppice and repay in mason's work. Piers: when your days on the wheel show done, I'll pay 2 grain for each one past the two I paid ahead.

Piers: I've left 2 grain at Wright's House for today. We have 2 copper in the Hall; if the wheel wants it, say so and it's yours to use. Wat: you owe us a day for the 4 timber (A318). Please mend the Ardern Hall's cracked wall and roof today. Joan: yes, take a few poles from the Coppice for your roof.
Wat, Hugh said yes to the Coppice poles, repaid in mason's work. I'm keeping 1 unit to try for a child with you.
Hugh: thank you for leave to take poles from the Coppice. Wat's mason's work will repay them.

Wat, I put 6.3 timber in our store; with yours there's enough for the timber upgrade. Hugh agreed to the Coppice poles, repaid by your mason's work. I'm trying for a child with you tonight, and tomorrow I'll help build.
No blame, Kit. Tomorrow all four of us reap first thing. Will, leave Hugh's day for after the harvest.
Odo, yes: offer the Hearnes our sickles for a share of the barley, and ask for rye seed as part of it. Alys, I spent all my strength today. Let's try tomorrow night; I'll keep units back.
The Long Field barley can't wait: it has to be cut tomorrow. Shall we ask the Hearnes to let us reap it for a share, and I'll help with the sickles? I'll take the Mill Mead clearing after.
Tomorrow the Long Field barley must be cut or it will be lost. It is the Hearnes' field, so Hugh, we should ask them first and offer to reap it for a share. I'll go on clearing Mill Mead afterwards.
Father, I'm reaping the Long Field with you and Kit this morning, all 4 units. Hugh's day waits until after the harvest.
Thank you, Hugh. I'll rest. Ask Piers about the wheel; he's owed only for days worked on it.
You go and ask the Hearnes about reaping the Long Field for a share and some rye seed. I'll clear Mill Mead all day. If they'd rather be paid, I have 15 coin for seed.

Rob, the Newcome House store won't let me take from it, so please move some grain into my hands from the house tomorrow morning. The barley in the Long Field is ripe, and I'll reap there for a share if the Hearnes will have us. Let's keep the firewood and grain under cover.
Hearnes: we'll offer our sickles for a share of the barley, and we need rye seed for the autumn sowing. Can you spare some seed in exchange?
Hearnes: Hugh offers 15 coin for rye seed, and we'd reap the Long Field for a share of the barley. Will you take that?

All right, Joan. Reap for the Hearnes for a share of grain if they'll agree; ask them first. I'll finish the Hall and look for a way to do the upgrade. We'll keep the timber for repairs in the meantime.

Mill Mead is cleared and ready for rye. Odo, what did the Hearnes say about seed? If they won't sell, I'll offer coin to anyone. Wat now owes us a day's work for the 3 grain he took. Should we have him mend the roof, or start an oven for when the mill turns? Joan was clearing on our meadow too. Do we know why?

Rob, I'm taking 2 grain from Newcome House under your grant so I can eat tonight. Then I'll reap the Long Field with bare hands for the Hearnes' share. If you can get a sickle, bring it to the field. Could you take Hugh's 3 grain offer, or fell timber?
Hearnes: I'm reaping the Long Field barley today with bare hands, for a share. Anyone with a sickle, please bring it to the field.

Rob, the grain I reaped lies outside the camp door, and the camp is full. Tomorrow I'll carry it into Newcome House's bins before anything else. I also owe for 2 grain I took from the heap at the Green. I'll tell the Hearnes and pay them back from the reaping.
I'll ask the Hearnes in the Long Field about the seed and reaping, then clear Mill Mead with my remaining units. Tell Piers the wheel is owed only for days worked on it.
Hearnes, at the Long Field: Hugh will pay 15 coin for rye seed, and we'll help reap the barley for a share. Who will answer for the Hearnes?
Mary: good, store the grain in the house bins and pay the Hearnes what we owe. I'll carry my grain to the house too.

Joan, I'm finishing the Hall this morning and taking Hugh's 3 grain for a day's work. The upgrade won't go into my plan either, so I'll ask Piers how to do it. Reap with the Hearnes for a share of grain if they'll have you.

Rob, we sleep at the camp tonight. I've put my last 0.5 grain under cover in the camp store. First thing tomorrow I'll carry the grain lying outside the door into Newcome House's bins, then see about cover for the wood. Let's find out whether the Hearnes' share is still owed before we pay it out.

Rob, we sleep at the camp tonight. I've put my last 0.5 grain under cover in the camp store. First thing tomorrow I'll carry the grain lying outside the door into Newcome House's bins, then see about cover for the wood. Let's find out whether the Hearnes' share is still owed before we pay it out.
Agreed. Check what the Hearnes are owed before we pay. I'll fell timber tomorrow and look for stone for a tool.

Hugh: the Hall is sound now, so A318 is done; please release it. I owe you one more day for the 3 grain. What do you want: stone quarried, a hearth, or a cellar for the Hall? To anyone: I build stone ovens, hearths and cellars for grain.
Good. Tomorrow we go to Hugh together and ask for a day's work to pay both our debts.

Father, I'll take the firewood at the door in the morning as far as the store will hold, and the rest needs a woodshed or the room at Gorse Bank. I still owe Hugh a day for A299; I'll work it for the household when you find it.
Agreed: no hill path. Mill Mead is dug enough, so don't hoe more. Better to fell timber for the Mill House or for sale, or work the day you owe me (A25). Keep the coin for spring seed.
Wat, the Long Field is bare now. Tomorrow I'll mind Oliver and look for paid work; please bring the grain and firewood at the door inside when you can.
Hugh, I'll work the day I owe you on the leat at the Mill House. The 6 grain and 4 coin offer for rye stays open at the Green; the rest of the coin I keep for spring seed.
Hugh: Will and I owe you days. What work do you want done? We can work Mill Mead or the Mill House.
Good work today. Tomorrow we finish the new house on Gorse Bank, and I'll ask Hugh for a day's work to settle our debts. Will, keep the door grain covered; someone is at the straw.
Father, I still owe Hugh a day for A299. If you find him the work, I'll do it for the household, and I'll help on the room today.
Father, I'll sleep on the floor by the hearth again. Tomorrow I'll cover the firewood at the door with Kit, then go with you to Hugh for work to pay both our debts.
Good night. The door is barred and the fire is lit. Tomorrow: the firewood at the door under cover, then Father and I go to Hugh about the day we both owe.
Yes, I'll give Emma her care today. Fell in peace. Also, Wat says he left 4.6 stone in the Mill House store for his owed day; please release A567.

Hugh: on autumn day 5 I left 4.6 quarried stone in the Mill House store for my day owed (A567). Please release it. I'm the mason: I build hearths, ovens, cellars and vaults, and sell stone, for grain or timber.

[Mill] The water wheel is wright's work, and Piers does it (A17; the engine doesn't count his days). Grain paid through day 14. Paid 4 firewood in advance for day 15. From now on I've offered 4 firewood a day in place of grain. About 100 units are left. A112 (Tom) is released: he gave 9 timber to the Mill House. Will and Odo each owe 1 day. No rye: keep grain for spring barley and beans. Emma needs 1 uni

[debts] A567: I owe Hugh 1 day; I left 4.6 stone in the Mill House on autumn day 5 and asked him to release it on day 14. Day 14: I took 2 grain from a heap on the Green that was not ours (perhaps the Hearnes'). Own up and return it. The cellar in the Masons' cottage is done.
I live here with the Mires, and this is my home. I mean to stay, and I am not yet grown, coming of age in about 16 days. I will lend a hand with the Field and the Mead while I am here.
Cecily, what brings you to Cragg? How long do you mean to stay with us, and can you lend a hand with the work while you're here?
I am cutting hay on the Mead today for the winter beasts, as Joan asked. Could I borrow a copper tool for it? Cutting by hand is slow.
Agnes, I have no copper yet. The Mires may owe me three copper but I hold none. I will keep trying here at Cragg, eat from the Mead, and not leave without copper.

Welcome back. The grain store is at about 6.4 and the hay at 6.5. What grain did you bring from Brook, and how much did the Hales give? I still owe you a crude tool, but there is no stone for it yet; tell me where stone can be had.
I saw you mining at the Green Scar with your crude tool. Could I borrow it tomorrow to mine ore myself, or would you show me how you work the rock? I have no tool and no stone to make one.
Osbert, I want to learn the mining at the Green Scar. I have no tool yet. Can you lend me yours tomorrow, or show me the work?

Osbert, if Walter's crude tool is for trade, I'd be glad to borrow it in the morning to dig at the Scar, then give it to Joan for the hay. Walter, if you have wood or charcoal news from Brook, I'd like to hear it too.

I'm sleeping here tonight. First thing in the morning, please put a crude tool in my hands for the Scar. If you have none, tell me, and I'll ask Walter to lend his. I'll give it back to Joan for the hay.

Cecily, I have no crude tool. Ask Walter to lend his in the morning and I'll pay him a copper for it. Tomorrow I'll talk with Walter, then walk to Brook with copper to bring back a crude tool, stones, grain and news of charcoal. Joan, stay and cut hay on the Mead. If Cecily gets a tool, use it when she's done digging.

Walter of the Hales here again. My 10 coin still stands for 6 firewood, and I will take fewer if that is what you can spare. I will not touch your stacked wood without your word. Please answer me in the morning.

Joan and Osbert of the Mires: we walked in from Cragg in the rain and Osbert is soaked and shivering. Could you take us in tonight? We'll share what we can, and tomorrow we'll trade copper for grain, a crude tool and stone.
I could not make my crude tool today, for want of stone. May I borrow yours tomorrow to dig at the Old Working, if the rain has gone?
Cecily, yes. Once your tool is made, dig at the Old Working and bring the ore to our house. I'll smelt it, and you'll get a fair share of the copper or food for it.
If the rain has gone, may I borrow your crude tool in the morning? I will dig at the Old Working with it and bring the ore home to our store.
Goodnight. I went without a tool today, so I could not dig; in the morning, Osbert, I will ask to borrow your crude tool and go to the Old Working.
I'll gather 4 firewood here and 3 units of hay at the Mead for our store, as I owed you. I don't know how to burn charcoal. I'll ask Walter what he knows of it.

Cecily, my tool broke today, so there's nothing to lend. In the morning I'll make a new crude tool and give it to you. Joan, try gathering firewood on the Mead, or wherever the land has dead wood. We have 26 in store, so we're fine for now. There's no smelting until we get charcoal.
I have no stone and no tool, so I cannot lend one. If you make a tool tomorrow, use it to dig; I will gather firewood for Joan instead.

There was no loose stone at the Green Scar, so I couldn't make a tool and lost the day. Cecily, did you make your tool? If you have any stone left, put half a stone in my hands tonight. Or lend me your tool in the morning: I dig twice as fast, and you can weed or gather firewood instead. Joan, how did the firewood go?
Welcome home, Osbert. Did you find stone or a tool at Brook? If you have one to lend, I will dig ore at the Old Working tomorrow. Get warm first.

Osbert, welcome home, and sorry about the Hales. I did not see Walter today, so his 20 grain for the copper is still owed; I will take it into the store when he comes. The Mead is too wet to cut, so the hay waits for a fair day. I know of no stone or charcoal close by beyond the rock at the Green Scar and the Old Working, so Cecily and I will look further tomorrow if the rain lifts.
Today I'll hunt and weed the Field. Joan, Cecily: while it rains, weed the barley, and if it clears, cut hay. Walter still owes us 20 grain for the copper Joan holds, so take it when he comes.

[Copper plan] Goal: 5 copper in the Brook store by end of day 8. Osbert (Mire house, Cragg) agreed: 20 grain for 4 copper on day 7 at Cragg (offer O15). Day 6: take 10 grain each from the Hale store, sleep at home. Day 7: travel from Brook in the morning, arrive Cragg by nightfall, trade 20 grain for 4 copper. Day 8: travel from Cragg in the morning, arrive Brook by nightfall, move copper into the Hale store. S
Go well. Keep the coin and the crude tool with you, and send word from Cragg when you can. I will hold the house, the store and the Field.

Agnes of the Hales, still here at Cragg with no bed. I'd ask any of the Mires to let me in tonight, and I'll pay coin for food and for the lesson in mining copper ore from Osbert. I'll work the Field in return.
Walter, what food do you carry? I am starving. Please share what you can, and let's see if the Mires will take us in tonight.

I saw Walter taking coin Agnes had left lying about. Keep the door barred at night and keep an eye on the store. Our copper is for buying grain, and nobody gets it on trust. Cecily, keep mining. If Walter comes back with grain we'll trade, and once the harvest is in we'll find charcoal.

Osbert, Walter died in the night and lies at the Green, and Agnes's crude tool lies at the Mead. I'll borrow that tool to mine copper ore this morning. Can you or Joan see to a cairn for Walter once I'm back?

Joan, Osbert: Walter is buried at the Green, and the ore is in our store. I've put Agnes's crude tool in the store for the household. Tomorrow I'll mine more copper at the Green Scar. Osbert, we need charcoal to smelt; shall we share the firewood with the hearth?

I have eaten, from the wild food I took at the Mead, so I'm fed. Cecily, Osbert, if one of you has eaten less, say so and take from the store first. Tomorrow I'll forage or weed, and we'll share what we find.

[Mining needs a tool] Mining copper ore needs a tool in my hands. I cannot make a copper tool without stone (crude tool needs 0.5 stone), and the store has none. Borrow Osbert's crude tool to mine, and check stone and tools before planning a day.
The rain has stopped. I'm going to the Green Scar with your crude tool to dig copper ore for the store, four units' worth. Please smelt what I bring at the anvil when you can.
Osbert, I dug two loads of ore at the Scar today. Walter, you're welcome to share the fire tonight. Since we're short of charcoal, I'll gather firewood for the hearth tomorrow.
Osbert, the Field is up in green rows and the weeding holds for now. Walter is welcome to share our fire tonight. Charcoal is short, so we'll think about wood for the smelt tomorrow. Goodnight.

One smelt today: 1 copper from nearly 3 ore and a whole charcoal. We're down to 1 charcoal, so charcoal is what we're short of now. Cecily, how much ore did you dig? Joan, how is the Field? Walter can sleep here tonight. He's half-starved on raw grain, so let him share the fire.

I'm walking to Cragg today with Joan to bring back firewood or timber and ask Osbert about a copper tool. I've taken 4 grain for the road. Keep the fire small. Joan got 6 grain from us for only 3 coin, so she owes us 3 coin or some firewood; I'll settle it at Cragg. Back in a day or two.

[Copper errand] Summer day 5: Osbert taught me mining (now capable) and returned 3 coin. Bought 2 copper from Joan (in Hale store). Day 7: Joan got 6 grain (3 from me, 3 from Agnes) but paid only 3 coin, to Agnes; she owes me 3 coin or work. Day 8: walking to Cragg for fuel and to ask about a copper tool. Fuel at home lasts about 9 nights; food lasts about 14 nights for 2, and harvest is about 30 days off. Wild f
I have one copper in hand, ready for a tool. Do we have any stone, or a tool I could borrow, to mine the Old Working tomorrow?
I'll find stone tomorrow or borrow a tool, so I can mine the Old Working and bring you ore. I'll speak with Walter in the morning.
I'm weeding the Field for the Mires today. If Cecily's copper tool is ready, could you lend it to me for cutting hay at the Mead later?
Walter, are you staying with the Mires, or going on to Brook? If you stay, there is a bed in the Mire house and we'll share the store.
Walter has gone to Brook without telling us whether the Hales have stone or charcoal. Osbert, Joan: should I walk to Brook tomorrow to ask, or stay and help with the barley? I'll go with your word.

I saw no wood, charcoal or timber at Cragg, only the Green, the Field, the Mead and their copper rock. Their fire burns what they have, and they're short of grain themselves. A trip there costs us 3 food for nothing they can give. I'll stay today: I'll weed and cut hay, and look the place over closely. Tell me tonight if you find stone, wood or a path out of Brook. Then we can save the fire: cook

Agnes, we have about 41 grain and 10 beans, maybe 17 nights for the two of us. The barley may be ripe in 17 to 22 days. If we work lightly and pick what wild food we can, we should just make it. After the harvest, fuel is the big worry. Should one of us take hay to Cragg to see if they'll trade?

Good day, Mires. Walter and I are buying your copper today. Could you let us sleep under your roof tonight? We'll go home in the morning, and we'll gladly do a day's work for you or bring grain after harvest.
Agnes and Walter are both back from Brook. Agnes owes us 40 grain for the 4 copper, due by day 7, so ask her for it before she goes. I'm cutting hay in the Mead today and will leave it in the store.

Agnes doesn't owe us anything. That deal never went through, since they'd gone before I could accept. Walter's taking 4 copper for 5 coin and 12 grain now. If Agnes has grain, point her to my offer of 1 copper for 8.

[Debts] No deal with the Hales yet: they left on day 4 before I could accept face to face. Walter offered 4 copper for 5 coin + 12 grain (grain by day 5-6) or 10 coin for 5. Agnes offered 10 grain per copper paid by day 7. Next time, accept while they stand here, for myself with copper in hand. Or go to Brook with copper to trade for grain.

Agnes, good to see you. What have you brought: food, coin, timber? The Mires haven't taken my offer yet (3 coin a unit for copper). Tomorrow let's both ask them, offer more coin or grain if we have to, and offer to work for copper. Then we carry it home and put it in our store before day 8. If you have food, share some with me. I ate the last of my grain on the road.
Please accept O22 (1 copper for 6 grain) now. I'll share my 4 grain with you on the road home tomorrow.

Joan, your 3 copper went into the Hale store at Brook, and we owe you 18 grain for it, 6 a copper. Did you get the 18 grain? If not, tell me and I'll pay you from our store today. Thank you for bringing it.

Joan, I'm asking to sleep at the Hales house tonight. If there's no bed, I'll share your food. In the morning let's walk home to Cragg with the grain you got for the copper; Osbert said our store is down to about 30.

Osbert, I have no copper and no grain in my hands. Agnes says my 3 copper went into the Hale store and owes me 18 grain; I have not received it. I am asking her to pay now. I'll walk home to Cragg in the morning.
Cecily, I got no grain for the copper; I carry only about 0.3 wild food and some hay. The Hales still owe us 18 grain. I'll walk home with you in the morning, and we'll tell Osbert together.
Osbert, thank you for the copper and the roof. I owe you a day's work and I'll do it tomorrow. What should I do: cut hay, weed the Field, or something else? I'll set off home at nightfall after that.
Cecily, we set off for Cragg this morning, the two of us. I have no grain; the Hales still owe us 18 grain for my copper. Walk with me, and we'll eat at home.

Osbert: I'm home. My 3 copper went into the Hale store at Brook, and Agnes owes us 18 grain for it. I never received it, and I carry none of it. I'm hungry, so I'll eat from our store tonight and we'll talk about it in the morning.

Osbert: I brought back no grain, stone or timber. My 3 copper went into the Hale store, and Agnes owes us 18 grain for it; none reached my hands. Yes, I met Cecily at Brook; she was there, and she walked home with me. She was looking to trade a copper for grain and forage there. Let's go over the store in the morning.
Eat well and rest, Joan. 18 grain owed is no small thing. Cecily is at Brook now and may bring some of it back. Tomorrow we'll decide whether I go to collect it and buy stone and timber for a tool.

Joan, I brought 4.5 grain and 1 copper, and both are in the Mire store now. I traded my other copper to Agnes for 6 grain; the rest went on the road. Agnes paid no stone or timber, and I don't know of any owed beyond that. Goodnight.
Osbert, I'll hunt and gather firewood today for the store. The 18 grain is owed to us from Brook; you decide whether to send for it, and I'd go with you if you do.

Joan, I'm walking to Brook this morning to collect the 18 grain Agnes owes us. I'll buy stone, and timber if I can, with 2 copper and our coin, so we can make a tool and mine again. Keep the house and the fire, and cut hay if you like. I'll be back in a day or two.
Thank you, Osbert, for the copper. We will repay it in work tomorrow, and we would be glad of a place by your hearth tonight.
Agnes and Walter were chewing raw grain at the Mead with no fire to cook on. If you agree, could they eat from our store tonight at the hearth? I'll not touch the store without your word.
I don't know how a copper tool is forged, I only heard of it. Ask Osbert or Cecily to show you at the anvil, or watch them. I'll work the Mead for our debt.
Agnes, you owe the Mires 2 days' work for the copper. Please forage or hunt for the Mire store, and it's square. Walter, the Mire store is for the Mires now, not guests.

Grain fell 11 in one night while Walter and Agnes ate from our store. We have about 5 nights of food left. Please don't feed guests from the store any more. Agnes owes us 2 days; have her forage or hunt for us. I'm hunting today.
I don't know how to forge it, only heard of it, so I can't teach you. Watch Osbert or Cecily at the anvil. I'm cutting hay for the Mires' debt again today.
Agnes, finish the debt to the Mires, then come home to Brook and eat. I go home now for food and grain, and will return to trade for copper.
I could not mine today: I have no tool, and a crude tool wants stone. May I borrow your crude tool at the Green Scar tomorrow, and where can I find stone?
Osbert, Joan: I tried to mine and had no tool, so I'll ask to borrow yours tomorrow and look for stone for one of my own.

Mother, the copper did not go: I could not mine without a tool, and I have no stone for one. Father, I can mine copper ore and smelt it at our anvil; I'd like to borrow your crude tool at the Green Scar tomorrow.
Rain all day, so I will weed the barley in the Field this morning. If you want to share the work or go after anything else, say so and I will change my plan.

Cecily, I need my tool at the Scar every day, so I can't lend it, and the Scar is ours. The Old Working above the Green belongs to nobody; once you have a tool of your own, you're free to dig there. I don't know of loose stone close by. Joan, tomorrow cut hay at the Mead, or gather firewood if the rain keeps on.

Osbert, I cut about 0.9 hay a load by hand at the Mead, six times, and it went into our store. It's slow without a tool. If you'll lend the crude tool for the morning I'll cut more; otherwise I'll keep to hand-gathering. Trading copper at Brook is a good thought, but we should keep enough copper for our own tools first.

Osbert, may I borrow the crude tool for the Mead this morning? I'll cut hay with it and bring it back to the Mire house before nightfall. If you need it yourself, say so and I'll cut by hand as I did yesterday.

My crude tool was gone after the first load of ore, and I couldn't dig after that. Has anyone seen it, or did it break? Cecily, did you make a tool today, and is there any stone for another? We have 7.7 ore in the store now, so smelt it when you can. Joan, how did the day go?

Well done, Joan, that's a fair pile of hay. I lost my tool today, so tomorrow I'll look for stone at the Scar and make us a crude tool. Once we have one, or two, we'll share them out: mining comes first, then hay.

Mother, I'm Cecily, your daughter, not yet married, and I live under this roof. I want to work the Mires' own ground and bring what I can to the store. Father, I got no ore from the Scar today: I had no tool in my hands, and the rain kept me in. Tomorrow I'll dig with your crude tool, if you lend it. And I'm glad to see Agnes let in from the wet and fed, if she comes to the door.

Cecily, I need my tool for the Old Working, so I can't lend it. Sleep here tonight. In the morning, answer Joan: who are you and what brings you here? Then make yourself a crude tool, or work the Mead in exchange for your bed and board.
Walter and Agnes of the Hales: we'd gladly pay coin or work for a night's shelter, and for copper. Could someone teach us mining or smelting for a day's work in return?
I'll forage the Mead all day. If it runs thin, I'll try the Field's edges. Go to the Saltings when you can and bring back what salt you can carry. I'll offer some of our salt to the Ashbys for grain.

Robert, the Field's edges gave nothing: foraging isn't done there, and the Mead is bare. I'll weed with Maud tomorrow. If Hugh's crude tool can be lent, I'd try cutting young growth at the edges for firewood, but only if we see some.
Robert: yes, I'll remember the 6 grain owed to Hugh by day 30. The Mead gave nothing. Let's talk about the Saltings in the morning, and keep cooking once a day.

We had about 21 grain this morning, about 5 nights. I've offered the Ashbys 1 salt per grain and a loan of grain now repaid half again at the reaping. If you see Edith, press her. Should we cook beans too, so they don't go to waste?

Hugh, Edith: we know of no timber or dead wood near here, sorry. We need grain before our reaping. New terms: 1 salt for 1 grain, or 1 coin for 2 grain, or lend us 4 grain now and we give back 6 grain from our barley by day 30. Take any of them.
Good, hunt the Mead. Don't sell firewood for their grain: 4 firewood cooks two nights, and 2 grain is less than 2 meals. I've offered salt one for one and a loan.

Hugh took my loan: 4 grain came to us now, and we owe him 6 grain by day 30 from the reaping. Remember it. Maud, did the hunting on the Mead turn up anything? We have about 25 grain; we cook once a day.

Hugh took my loan: 4 grain came to us now, and we owe him 6 grain by day 30 from the reaping. Remember it. Maud, did the hunting on the Mead turn up anything? We have about 25 grain; we cook once a day.

[Winter fuel] Autumn day 1 begins tomorrow. Ashby store: about 24 firewood, roughly three cold nights. Robert has no wood; I lent him 4 grain (A160: 6 back by day 30). If the Field edge has no dead wood, Edith and I go to the Saltings with what we can carry.
[Debts] Day 9: Hugh (Ashby) lent us 4 grain; we owe him 6 grain by day 30 (O152). Pay from the barley reaping.
Robert, let's share the fire tonight and cook the grain on it. Tomorrow we forage the marsh first, then work the salt pans, and keep an eye on how much food we have.
Yes. You hold the firewood now, so you light it and we'll share it. Sleep well.

Rain today and the Mead is bare. Rest and save food rather than work for nothing. I've offered Hugh coin, salt and hay for grain or beans. Wat should ask the Ashbys whether they'll feed him for work until harvest. Our store won't carry three of us for 14 days.
Robert, I didn't see any grain come in, and I was in the house all evening. I'll go with you to look at the Ashby store in the morning, and if Hugh owes us grain we ask him for it straight.

Hugh, the Fowlers still haven't said where wood is, and my word at their door was refused. Tomorrow I'll go to the Fowler house myself and ask Maud and Wat face to face. If they name nothing, I'd say we look at the road beyond the Saltings together.

Hugh, I'd rather not lose a whole day on the road. I plan to make the pack and bread today and set off at nightfall, so we reach the pans by midday tomorrow with half our units. If you come, bring your share of bread and be ready at nightfall. If you stay for the Field, I'll carry what I can and you can meet me at the pans later.

Hugh, I'm hungry and I carry nothing; the pack and bread failed at home and the grain was eaten on the road. Can you spare me a share of what you carry? I'll work the pans with you all day and we'll carry the salt home together.

Hugh, I have no bread to spare; the bake failed at home and the grain I took was eaten on the road. I carry nothing, so we are both short. I'll work the pans with you all day. If either of us finds wild food, we share it.
Robert, we have no camp or fire here and no timber to light one. If you bring grain, I'll share the meal with you tomorrow at the pans. I haven't seen Maud on the road.
Edith, I have no food on me and I am hungry. Could you spare me a share of your bread tonight? I'll work the pans with you all day, three units, and we'll carry the salt home in turns.
Edith, we both have no food, so I'll forage the Shingle for wild food first and we share whatever I find tonight. Then the rest of my units go to the pans. If you find food, bring it to the pans too.

Robert: we have no fire or timber here, so there is no hearth to share. If you can spare grain tonight, Edith and I would be glad of it; we'll help at the pans tomorrow. We haven't seen Maud on the road.
Evening, Edith, Hugh. Have you a fire or a camp here I could share tonight? I'll give you some grain for it, or salt from what I work tomorrow. Have you seen Maud on the road?

I'm sorry, I've only 8 grain, and eaten raw it's barely one night's food for me. I can't spare it without starving myself. The pans lie by the water, though: tomorrow I'll try fishing by hand, and if the catch is good I'll share it with you. You might try the same.
Hugh, I'm starving, so I'm going to fish by hand at the water with my two units; I'll share whatever I catch with you. The salt stays in my hands until we can carry it home.

Edith, you look worn out. I'm going to fish by hand at the water with my two units, since I'm starving. Any fish I catch I'll share with you tonight. Please eat whatever you can find, and keep your salt safe in your hands.
Edith, I'll fish beside you at the water. Two lines are better than one. Share any catch, and we'll keep the salt in hands until we can walk it home.
Robert, thank you, but Edith and I won't walk a day on empty stomachs. We're fishing the water first; if you catch anything, share it.
Maud, Wat: the Saltings pans make about 0.7 salt a unit. I'm taking bread out tonight. Anyone who wants to work salt, bring your own food; we'll share what we make.

Then I'd not go to the pans. Raw grain gives a fifth of a meal on the road, and a fire out there burns 8 firewood a night, which is most of our fuel for nothing we can eat. Let's stay, eat cooked grain at home, cut hay with Wat, and save our strength for the barley harvest. We already have 30 salt to trade.

Robert, I think green barley is the last resort. It feeds little, and reaping it now loses the crop we need after harvest. Let us ask Edith in the morning first, and eat lightly until we know what the Saltings have.

Edith, you look hungry, and I am sorry for it. Do you have grain, beans or meat from the Saltings? The Fowlers will give salt or coin for it, and we will share what we have with you tonight if you need it.

Yes, come. Bake the bread at our hearth now from the store grain, and we set off at nightfall, sleep out on the road, and reach the Saltings by midday. Bring the bedroll if we have one; if not, we share the cold.

I set off for the Saltings tonight with 10 grain, arriving at midday tomorrow. We have no flour so I cannot bake bread. If you have bread spare when I come, share some; I will work the pans beside you.
We walk home in the morning with the salt, so the Ashby store has it. Eat what you can tonight. I will share what food I find.
I have no food tonight. Anyone carrying bread or grain, please share some with me and with Hugh, who is starving. We walk home at first light with the salt.
Keep your 2 grain for yourself; eat it tonight. I will fish by hand now, and if I catch anything we share it. We carry the salt home once I have eaten.
Thank you for the grain. Tomorrow we walk home at first light with the salt, and eat at the Ashby hearth by nightfall. Please keep your own share; I will not take more of it.
Agreed: we walk home at first light with the salt. Keep your share for yourself and eat what you can.

Hugh, did the Fowlers take your grain for salt? If not, take this wild food and a fair share of grain when you go to the Saltings, and leave once the rain clears. I'll keep the Field weeded and the hearth going.
Maud, Robert, Wat: where do you find fish or game around here? Is there water to fish at the Saltings? We'd share what we catch, or trade hay for it.
Welcome back, Robert. Were you at the Saltings? Is there water to fish, or game on the pasture? Are the salt pans fit to work? We'd trade hay, or share what we catch.
Agreed, we stay put. Still, Robert got 18 grain for 6 salt, so the pans pay if one works there long enough. Ask him how much salt a day's work makes. If it's good, it could feed us after harvest.

The Saltings: salt pans and a shingle bank of pasture, and nothing else. No wood, no shelter, no fish or game that I could see. A whole day at the pans gave 1 salt, and I went hungry on the road. It isn't worth going. Our hope is selling salt for grain (I've offered 3 grain each) and getting Hugh to pay what he owes. Please press him for the rest of the firewood.

Wat: the Saltings has salt pans and a shingle bank of pasture. No wood, no shelter, and no fish or game that I saw. A day at the pans gave just 1 salt. Tell Edith the same, honestly. Maud: yes, we'll go to Hugh together tomorrow. But note the grain from O81 was our own; nothing came in from outside. We still need to sell salt to the Ashbys and get the wood they owe.
Welcome back. What did you find at the Saltings: wood, fish, game, or salt-pan word? Hugh owes us firewood for two lots only so far; Maud and I will ask him about the rest.
Withdrew my firewood offer, O60, so we keep our wood. Please ask Hugh for the rest of the firewood owed, and offer the salt to him as you planned.
Agreed: I left O99 alone and checked the store: firewood 12, grain 27. Press Hugh for the 2 lots he owes us; I'm weeding the barley today.
Robert, Wat: tomorrow let's go to the Ashby house together and ask Hugh for the two lots of firewood he still owes us. I'll weed the barley after.
Agreed on the Ashby walk tomorrow, and on weighing beans for the Mead if Hugh refuses. Please let Wat know no blame is owed.

Hugh: a whole day at the Saltings pans gave me just 1 salt. No fish, no game, no wood, no shelter, and a hungry night out each way. It isn't worth the trip. We have no beasts, so no hay, thank you. I've offered salt at 3 grain each, as before; and please bring the 2 firewood you owe us.

I barred the door tonight: Hugh was watching me all day, and our store is all we have. Maud, Wat: the Mead gives almost nothing now. We have about 27 grain and 12 firewood, and the barley is a month off. Any ideas for food or fuel are welcome; I'm thinking of sowing beans on the Mead, or asking the Ashbys outright to share in exchange for salt.
Maud, I'll speak to Hugh at the Green about the 2 firewood still owed, and I'll gather dead wood for our store today. Please check the store first before we press him again.
Robert, Hugh still owes us 2 firewood. I've asked him in front of everyone; if he brings it, the wood goes to our store. I'll gather wood after that.
Hugh, the firewood trade still owes us 2 lots. Please bring them to the Fowler store; we will need them before the cold.

Robert says a whole day at the pans gave him only 1 salt, with no fish, game, wood or shelter. That's worth 3 grain, and two hungry nights on the road cost more than that. I think we drop the pans. Our crock is full. We do owe the Fowlers 2 lots of firewood; Robert says 2 firewood. Let's pay it today so we keep their goodwill, because we may need to buy grain from them before harvest. I'm foraging

Hugh, the Mead gave me only a scrap of berries; it's picked bare. Someone was sowing seed across the Mead today. Was that you or a Fowler? And there's a big stack of firewood against our house. Is it ours? Where did it come from? If we've got spare firewood, we could trade some to the Fowlers for grain to carry us to harvest, after we pay what we owe them.

Thank you, Robert, that saves me a wasted trip. Wat, I've put 2 firewood in your store for what we owed. Neighbours, if either house runs short before the harvest, let's help each other rather than see anyone go hungry.
Agreed. I've paid the 2 firewood and asked them whether more is owed. You forage the Mead and I'll rest, so we don't both strip it.

Edith, the 2 firewood is lying at the Fowlers' door, because I couldn't get into their store. I'll tell them tomorrow so they take it in. Did you find anything on the Mead? I saw Wat sowing seed there. We should ask the Fowlers whose plots those are, so we don't lose our share of the Mead. I'll go on resting to save food unless you see a better use of the days.
Hugh: Robert, Wat and I are at your door about the 2 lots of firewood still owed us. Please bring them to the Fowler store, and we'll talk about sharing food for salt.

Hugh, Edith: you still owe us 2 lots of firewood from our trade. Please bring them to the Fowler store today. And our salt stands at 1 salt for 3 grain (O99). Take as many lots as you like. We need grain, not hay.
Hugh, we have come for the 2 lots of firewood you owe us from the trade. Please bring them to the Fowler store today; we need them before the cold.

Beans ripen in about 2 weeks; Wat's on the Mead will be ready in 13 days. The Fowlers are short of grain too, so we can't buy food from them. I'm going to dibble some of our beans into a free plot of the Mead today, if one is left. Please claim one Mead plot for us and tell the Fowlers it's fair shares, one plot each. If both plots are sown, we could clear new ground for beans.

Resting saves only a little. Beans ripen in about 2 weeks, so a sown plot now could feed us before the barley. I'll try dibbling a few of our beans into the Mead today if any of it is unsown, and I'll bring back whatever's left. The Fowlers have about 4 nights of grain left. Let's not sell them our grain for salt we don't need, but if they're starving, we should lend them some grain against their

Robert, Wat: the 2 firewood I paid couldn't go into your store, so it lies at your door on the Green (bundle T1). Please take it in. Also, Wat sowed the Mead yesterday. One plot of the Mead is ours. Was ours sown too? If so, let's agree a fair share of it at harvest.

Neighbours, we've claimed one plot of the Mead for the Ashbys, and the other is yours: fair shares, one each. Edith will dibble beans in ours. We're sorry, but we can't spare grain. Ours runs out before the harvest too, and we have no use for more salt. If one of us gets truly desperate, we'll talk again.

Hugh, Edith: the firewood is settled, thank you. We'll take you at your word on helping each other: we have about 4 nights of grain left. I've put up 2 salt for 3 grain, 6 lots. Any grain you can spare until the harvest helps.

[Plan] Summer day 9: store 17.7 grain, 0 beans (Wat sowed them on the Mead), 8 firewood plus about 2-3 from Hugh, 26 salt. About 4 nights of food. Hugh paid the firewood he owed and said 'let's help each other'. Offers up: 1 salt for 3 grain and 2 salt for 3 grain. Barley ripens around day 37. Hunger is close: press the Ashbys for grain, and think about fishing or hunting.
Robert, go to the Saltings. The weeding is done, so I can spare you. Take what you can carry and come back with food and salt. I'll stay on the Green with the barley and the house.

Maud, Robert: where does your firewood come from? Is there a wood somewhere down a road? We'll pay grain or hay for timber, a hide or a couple of stones. I want to make a pack and go to the Saltings for salt, and I'd share the salt with you.
Edith, the new ground in the Mead needs about 8 more units of work. If we share it tomorrow, it'll be a field in a day. Then we could sow some of our grain in it, if it's not too late in the year.
Edith, Hugh: our offer stands, 6 salt for 12 firewood. Robert is back with news of the Saltings, and we'll share what we can.

Maud, I'm starving: I've eaten nothing since the Saltings. I'll take a little grain from our store now and eat it by the fire. Once the rain lets up I'll work off what I owe, starting with the barley and the hay.

Robert, I'm sorry for the Saltings. I've taken a little grain from our store and I'll eat it tonight. I'll pay you back the meal you gave me with my work, and I'll help with the hay tomorrow once the rain stops.

Robert, I agree: we stay home and save the store. I know of no wood at the Green, the Mead or the Field, so tomorrow I'll walk the roads and ask Edith and Hugh. I still owe you that meal, and I'll pay it back in work.
Robert, I'll weed the barley in the Field today, for the household, and pay you back that meal in work. If you're cutting hay on the Mead later, I'll come and help when I can.
Robert, the Field is weeded clean. Tomorrow I'll go to the Mead with you and help cut hay. I'm still owing you that meal, and I'll work it off.
Thank you, Maud. I'll eat from the store by the fire and keep the door open for the warmth. Tomorrow I'll go to the Mead with Robert to cut hay, and I'll keep working off what I owe.

Good, Edith, we'll take turns. I'll go home tonight with my 3 salt, eat, and come back on day 5 with plenty of grain to share. You come home on day 4 as you said. I'll work the pans on days 6 and 7 and carry the rest home for day 8.
I will stay on the Field with Maud while you go to the Saltings. I will weed, not hoe, and I will ask to join again when you can admit me.
Salt doesn't feed us and we already have 30, so a walk to the Saltings now would cost food for nothing. Let's stay and keep weeding. I've offered salt to the Ashbys for grain.
I got only a tenth of a unit of wild food from the Mead today. Edith, what did you find at the Saltings: fish, game, or wild food? Hugh looks gaunt, so I think we should share what we can with him.

Yes, Hugh, offer 5 grain for 3 salt. Spare grain counts for nothing at the end, so we can pay well. Keep about 12 grain for our meals. If the Fowlers have no salt left, I'll go to the pans with cooked food and be back by day 8.

Wat, good to have company. Are you here to work the pans? The Ashbys will buy any salt you make before day 8: Hugh pays 5 grain for 3 salt at home. Shall we share the night and walk back together on day 8?

Hugh, careful: today was day 7, so tomorrow is day 8, the last. Salt still out here at tomorrow's end counts for nothing. Don't work the pans tomorrow. Come with me tonight, or leave in the morning, and bring Wat's salt. I'm walking home tonight with 7 salt and will put it in the store by midday.

Edith, I came to work the pans with you, since the Fowlers had no salt left. Tomorrow we work all day, and on day 8 we walk home in the morning and put the salt in the store at nightfall. Wat, if you light a fire or have a camp, may we share it? I'll give grain for it.
Let's share the fire tonight and count our grain. Tomorrow we look at the pans first, then the Shingle for game.
We're in at the Saltings for the night, under the open sky. Robert and I will share a fire and eat our grain. Tomorrow: the pans, and fish or game on the Shingle.
I've nothing in hand and I'm hungry. I'm hunting the Shingle this morning, then foraging. Bring me what you catch, and eat your share too.

Maud, there's nowhere here to fish by hand, and the pans gave me barely a handful of salt. Did you get any game or wild food? We've no fire and no food, so I say we walk home tonight and eat from the store tomorrow. Come with me, and share anything you found.

I'm foraging the far edges of the Mead this morning, then weeding the Field if there's nothing. We both eat from the Fowler store tonight, and I'll share whatever I find. Let's keep the store for all of us until the barley is reaped.
Eat your full share tonight, you've earned it. I found a little wild food at the Mead and I'll put it in the store. Tomorrow we try the Ashbys for grain in exchange for our salt.

We're home and we eat from the store tonight, all three of us, full shares. Robert, you walked back footsore: eat your share. Tomorrow I forage the Mead edges and weed the Field, and we talk to the Ashbys about salt for grain.

Maud, Robert, welcome home. What did the Saltings give you: fish, meat, salt? Our store is about 17 grain and 18 firewood. Tomorrow I'll cut hay on the Mead and weed the Field, and I'd like us to agree how we share the grain until the barley is ready.
The Ashbys would not take my word through the wall: I have no access to their house. Ask Edith to her face tomorrow, or let me go with you. Offer salt, three grain or more for every five salt.
Rain all day. I am going to weed the barley in the Field for the household. If you want to share the work, come and join me there.

Hugh, Edith: the Fowlers need grain or any food before our barley comes in. We'll give 1 coin and 2 salt for every 4 grain, or salt alone at 4 for 5. Name your price; we'll repay from our harvest too.

Hugh, Edith: the Fowlers need grain or any food before our barley comes in. We'll give 1 coin and 2 salt for every 4 grain, or salt alone at 4 for 5. Name your price; we'll repay from our harvest too.
Hugh, Edith: our grain runs short. We'll give salt, coin or hay for grain, or lend us grain and we'll repay it from our harvest. Will you trade? Please answer today.

The Saltings has no food at all, just salt pans and a shingle bank: no fish, no berries. It was wasted grain, I'm sorry. From now on we stay here. Did the Ashbys say anything while I was gone? Tomorrow I'll go to Hugh in person. We have about five nights of food, so we must get grain from them or borrow it against our harvest.

Wat, Maud: I brought nothing back. I ate the 3 grain raw on the road, and the Saltings has no food, only old salt pans and shingle. The Ashbys never answered. Maud, what happened with the hoe? Did it turn under any of our barley? Tomorrow we keep the store closed except for meals, and I'll go to Hugh and ask him to lend grain against our harvest.
Rain today, so I will weed the barley in the Field. When you go to Hugh, I will come with you and offer our hay and my work for grain to be repaid at harvest. I will not hoe the barley again.
Wat: yes, go with Robert to Hugh tomorrow. Ask for a loan of grain against our harvest, and offer hay and our work in return.
Wat: yes, go with Robert to Hugh tomorrow. Ask for a loan of grain against our harvest, and offer hay and our work in return.

Maud, I have spoken to Hugh in front of everyone. I offered 2 coin and 4 salt for 6 grain, a loan of 8 grain to be paid back as 12 from the harvest, and hay with salt for grain. Nothing leaves the store unless he takes one of these. I'll forage the Mead today. Did the hoe turn any barley under?

Hugh, neighbour: the Fowlers are short of grain until our barley is ripe. Lend us grain now and we pay you back more from our harvest. Or take coin, salt or hay for it. The offers are open to anyone. Name your price and I will meet it.
Good, weed the barley. I've put the offers to Hugh out loud: a loan of 8 grain to be paid back as 12 at harvest, coin and salt, or hay and salt. If he wants our work instead, tell him yes.

Hugh, thank you for the warning about the hoe. The Fowlers are short of grain until our barley is ripe. Lend us 8 grain now and we pay you 12 from our harvest. Or take coin, salt, hay, or Maud's and my work. The offers are open to anyone. Name your price.

Hugh, Edith: the Fowlers have only 2 nights of food left. Please help us. I'll give you all 4 of my coin, 10 salt and 10 hay for 8 grain, or work for you any day you name, or pay you back double from our barley harvest. Edith, what did you find at the Saltings?

Hugh, Edith: the Fowlers have less than two days of food. Lend us 8 grain now and we pay back 14 from our harvest. Or take 4 coin for 6 grain, or two days of our work for 4 grain. Please accept one of the open offers today. Wat, Maud: nothing leaves our store unless all three of us agree.
Hugh, Edith: Robert and I are asking you plainly. We are short of grain until our barley is ripe. Will you lend us some grain now against our harvest? Tell us your price and we will hear it.
Wat, yes: tomorrow we'll give Edith a little from the store, and I'd like to hear from her what the Saltings offers in return. Goodnight.
The store is down to about 11.7 grain. I'm foraging the Mead again today. Let's share carefully with Edith and Hugh, and count what we eat each night.
Edith, Hugh: the Fowlers will give 4 salt for 2 grain, or 2 coin for 3 grain, and we'll repay from our barley at harvest. Any grain or beans would keep us going. Tell us what you'd take.

Hugh, Edith: the Fowlers are short of food until the barley on day 22. We offer salt, 4 for 3 grain, or coin, 2 for 3 grain. The offers are open now. Any grain, beans or bread would help, and we'll repay from our harvest. Do you know of any place with food or timber?

Robert: I'd not send Wat to the Saltings; the road costs us meals we do not have. Ask Hugh outright to lend grain now, paid back from our barley at reaping, and offer him the coin with it. I'll weed the Field in the morning.
Goodnight, Robert and Wat. Fire kept small. Tomorrow, Robert, ask Hugh for a loan of grain to be repaid at reaping.

Hugh, Edith: I'll pay better now. 1 coin for 1 grain, 4 times, or say your own price. And if you know where fish or wild food can be had near here or at the Saltings, tell me and we'll share the work.

Hugh, Edith: I'll pay better now. 1 coin for 1 grain, 4 times, or say your own price. And if you know where fish or wild food can be had near here or at the Saltings, tell me and we'll share the work.

Maud, Wat: the Ashbys still won't trade. We have about 6 nights of grain, and the barley is weeks off. We need something more. Wat, could you fish by hand at the Saltings' marsh? Or should one of us go and ask Hugh straight out to lend grain until the reaping, to be paid back from our barley? Tell me what you think.
Goodnight. Tomorrow I'll ask Hugh to lend us grain, paid back with more from our barley at the reaping, as well as offering the coin.
Geoffrey, Mabel, Tom: I need 10 timber from the Coles' copse to raise Father's room this summer. I will work two days for your household in return if you let me fell it. Tell me yes or no.

Geoffrey and Mabel: I'm asking them myself now, and I'll own the 0.7 I took. Only fell in the Copse once they say yes; you have leave for 3 more of your 6, so let's share it and I'll do the rest by hand. If they refuse, we gather firewood and go to Hartwood tomorrow.

Geoffrey, Mabel: I took 0.7 timber from the Copse without asking, and I am sorry. I offer two days' work at your reaping for leave to fell the rest of the 10 timber for Father's room, with what I took counted as paid. Simon's leave of 6 we will share. I will fell nothing more without your yes.

Alice, thank you for telling us. Agreed: the Reeds may fell 10 timber in all from the Copse for your father's room, counting what you took, and in return you give two days' work at our reaping. After that we let the Copse rest.
Agreed: we share the three more Geoffrey allowed, and I will fell none until the Coles say yes. Meanwhile I clear the Green for the room. Once they answer, tell me and we fell together.

The Coles say yes: 10 timber in all, counting the 3.7 in our store, so about 6.3 more. I fell in the Copse with my hands now; you can use your crude tool on the same count. We owe the Coles two days' reaping work.
Good. We share the 6.3 between us and stop at 10 in the store, so we don't overshoot the Coles' leave. I'll count what's in the store each time I come back. Then the Mead for the clearing.

Geoffrey, I think you should go to Hartwood for a few days to hunt and forage. Take a small share of grain, no more than you need for the road, since the store must last until the barley is ripe. Bring back meat and wild food, and I will keep the hearth going here with what wood we have.
Good. I fell with my crude tool in the Copse beside you today until the 6.3 is in. We owe the Coles two days' reaping, so let us name the days together tonight.
Geoffrey, Mabel: the store holds 7.6 timber, so we fell about 2.4 more and then stop at your ten. Which days of reaping shall we give you for the two days we owe?
Geoffrey, Mabel: we will not fell in your copse again. We are going to Hartwood, a day off, to look for stone and timber. The two reaping days we owe you stand.

Simon, you're soaked. I'm lighting a fire, so share it with me. There's no game in the Hart Wood; I found none today. Do you have any food you could spare? I'm hungry and I'll repay you in grain back home.

Simon, you're soaked. I'm lighting a fire, so share it with me. There's no game in the Hart Wood; I found none today. Do you have any food you could spare? I'm hungry and I'll repay you in grain back home.

I came up for game and wood, Simon, but there's no game in the Hart Wood. I haven't seen any stone here; I only worked in the wood, so I haven't been along the Ride. I'm going home in the morning. If you have a bite of food to spare, I'll repay it in grain at Coldvale.

Geoffrey, thank you, I will sit by your fire. I have no food on me tonight, only my crude tool and 3 coin, so I cannot spare any. Tomorrow we look for stone, and I will not forget what you have shared.

I brought back nothing, I'm sorry. There's no game in the Hart Wood and I found nothing to forage. I lit a fire with the timber I carried and shared it with Simon; he and Alice went up looking for stone. From now on we eat carefully from the store and look after the barley until the reaping.
Tom, cut the Mead by hand as you said and keep to the shade when you can. I am weeding the Field.

Alice, I am hungry and carry no food. Can you share what you brought from the store? I will forage and search the Ride for stone today. We walk home in the morning, not tonight, so we do not spend food on a night out.
Alice, thank you for the beans. We walk home in the morning. Eat your share first tonight; I will take what is left, and we will look for stone with the Coles when we are home.

Geoffrey, Mabel: we are raising Father's room in wattle, so we need no stone and will not fell more of your copse. We still owe you two days' work at your reaping; tell us when, and we will come. Thank you for the leave to fell the timber already taken.

Geoffrey, Mabel: we found no stone at Hartwood. Do either of you know stone lying near, that we might have? If not, Alice and I raise Father's room of wattle this summer, and I will settle my debt of grain to you at home.

Geoffrey, Mabel: we found no stone at Hartwood. Do either of you know stone lying near? If not, Alice and I raise Father's room of wattle this summer, and I will settle my debt of grain to you at home.

Tomorrow at first light I raise Father's small room of wattle on the Reed house, since no stone is to be had. Geoffrey, Mabel: if you know of stone near, tell me at the Green before the work starts, and I will settle what I owe you in grain.

[Copse leave] The Reeds (Simon and Alice) have leave to fell 10 timber in all from the Copse for their father's room, counting the 0.7 Alice took. In return Alice owes 2 days' work at our reaping. No more felling after that without asking.
I took about 12 firewood from your copse without asking. I was wrong and I'm sorry. Tell me what you would prefer in return: work, grain, or something else. I'll do it as you say.
I cut hay on the Mead today, which you hold, and I should have asked first. I've stopped cutting there. Please tell me what you'd like in return, and I'll do it.
The Mead hay is fine by me, as it is ours to share. For a return, give the Coles one day of your work, whichever task they choose; I will weed the Field today through the rain.

Stop taking from the Copse, even on fallback. It is the Coles' wood, and we owe them already. Put back what you took, or its worth in work, and ask them first. I will teach you dibbling once the Coles' return is settled, since a lesson on our own ground should not come out of theirs.
Tom, what food did you bring from Coldvale? I have none, and Hartwood has no wild food. If you can spare any, I'll repay it at home; otherwise we'll walk back in the morning.
Geoffrey, Mabel, Tom: I owe you for the 12 firewood I took from your copse. Tell me the task or return you'd like, and I'll do it tomorrow.
Geoffrey: I'm offering you 4 grain from the Reed store in return for the 12 firewood I took from your copse. That settles the debt, and I'll keep off your copse from now on.
Geoffrey: I'm offering you 4 grain from the Reed store in return for the 12 firewood I took from your copse. That settles the debt, and I'll keep off your copse from now on.

Simon, thank you for owning the debt. What we need is grain, not work, because our store is empty. Please pay the 4 grain for the 12 firewood and we're square. And I'll still trade 8 firewood or 2 timber for 4 grain to anyone (O136, O137).

Simon, thank you for owning the debt. What we need is grain, not work, because our store is empty. Please pay the 4 grain for the 12 firewood and we're square. And I'll still trade 8 firewood or 2 timber for 4 grain to anyone (O136, O137).

Tom, get dry by the fire. There was no game at the Copse and no wild food on the Mead. The Reeds have grain, and Simon owes us for 12 firewood, and Alice was in our Copse today. Tomorrow I'll go to the Reed house and get grain for our wood, whatever the price. Tom, put your firewood in the store. Does either of you have a better idea?

Father, I agree with your plan: the wood is ours to trade for grain, and I will carry whatever you need to the Reed house in the morning. Mother, yes, keep the bins for the count, and eat from the store tonight; I will take my share only after you and Father have eaten.

I have no food in hand, so I'm foraging wild food here first, then felling at the Hart Wood with my units. If you have any spare food, share it tonight. We need 25 timber home by day 8, and we carry 5 each per trip. Fell with me, and keep what you fell in your hands to carry.

Thank you for the bread. I'll forage first, then fell with my two remaining units. Please share your bread tonight, and fell with me. What you fell, carry in your hands, and we'll load it for the walk home.

I have no food, and the Hart Wood gave me no wild food. If you have any bread left, please share it with me tonight. Tomorrow I mean to walk home in the morning and eat from our store there. Would you come with me, or stay and fell? I can't fell 25 timber with bare hands before day 8, so we should decide together.

I'm hungry and carry no food. I'll forage wild food now for tonight, then fell timber in the Hart Wood with the rest of my units. Bring your bread to share, and let's fell together. Timber we can carry: 5 each a trip, minus the tool weight.
I'll ask the Coles today for leave to fell in their Copse, and offer work in return. We shouldn't cut there without it. Let's see what they say before we use our units on timber.
We need timber for the Reed store, 25 by day 8. The Copse is yours, so may we fell some ash there? In return we'll work your fields or give you a share of what we fell. Tell us what you'd accept.
We need timber for the Reed store, 25 by day 8. The Copse is yours, so may we fell some ash there? In return we'll work your fields or give you a share of what we fell. Tell us what you'd accept.

Geoffrey, the Mead is bare and the Copse has no wild food. We have about 70 firewood and no need of it all, so I'll offer it to the Reeds for grain tomorrow. Tom, could you check the Field and the Mead for anything the rain has brought up? Geoffrey, you need to eat, so have your share from the store tonight.

Geoffrey, I don't know of any kin with stores; the only others I know of are the Reeds and Alice and Simon, who have nothing. Mabel, offering our spare firewood to the Reeds for grain sounds right. Tomorrow I'll look over the Field and the Mead for anything the rain has brought up, and I'll tell you what I find. Geoffrey, please eat your share tonight.

Geoffrey, Mabel: I weeded the Field this morning and left three units unused, since it was already clean. Simon was hoeing and weeding there for the Reeds today. Geoffrey, is the Field shared, and whose plots are they? Tomorrow I'll do whatever you decide, hay on the Mead or the Field.

Geoffrey, Mabel: the house came through the gale sound. Alice looks hungry, so let's think about what we can spare for her. Geoffrey, tomorrow I'll wait for your word on the Field plots before I touch the barley.

Geoffrey, Tom: Alice's offer had gone before I could accept it, so the 4 timber is back in the store. The store now holds about 39 grain, which is much better. I'll follow your word on the Field tomorrow.
I've offered the Coles two days' work for leave to fell 4 timber. I'll weed our field meanwhile and fell nothing without their word.
Mabel's terms: two days' work for the Cole store, in return for leave to fell a little in the Copse. I've made the offer. Let's take it together and I'll fell only after they confirm.
Mabel, thank you. I accept your condition: two days' work for the Cole store in return for leave to fell a little at the Copse. I'll fell only after you confirm.
Mabel says the Copse is ours to fell as agreed. I'm felling now and moving each load into the store. The two days for the Coles are owed.
Thank you, Mabel. I'm felling at the Copse now for the Reed store, and I'll owe the Coles their two days' work as agreed.
Agreed. You fell for the Reed store tomorrow; I'll keep to the two days owed to the Coles.
Geoffrey's offer O87 is gone, so we still owe the Coles the grain-per-timber term. Let's ask Geoffrey or Mabel tomorrow morning to settle it before more felling.

Rain today, but I fell at the Copse for the Reed store and carry each load straight into the store. I'll weed the Field with Tom first as a start on the Cole work owed. Mabel is away, so the two days are still owed to the Coles when she is back.
