Edric, I gave Sibyl 4.5 timber for the Reeds to settle my bread debt. Do you need more timber? We have plenty, and I'd trade it for grain, seed grain especially, to sow this spring.

Of course, Edric, take your 8 and we'll keep the other 3 safe for you. I'm also giving Sibyl 4.5 timber of my own today, separate from yours, to repay the bread Odo and Isolde gave me this winter. When the barley's in, I'd like seed grain for timber.

Edric, Sibyl: you can't carry my 4.5 timber, so I'm adding it to the Reed timber we keep in Fenn House. After Edric takes his 4 today, 11.5 timber there belongs to the Reeds, and my bread debt is paid. Edith, please keep that count.

I'm home and putting 3 timber in the Reed store (I kept 1 to make a crude tool). Sibyl carries 4 more. The Fenns keep 11.5 timber for us: my 7 and Simkin's 4.5, which pays his bread debt. Please witness the stone with Tiffany today.
Alard, you have the copper tool. Fell with it while you can. When Warin is ready to mine, lend it to him on his promise of a copper tool back by about day 25.
Warin, mine well with our copper tool. Remember you owe a copper tool back to the Fenns by about day 25 (A232). Bring it here, and we'll feed you while you're in Ashwood.
Agreed, we leave tomorrow evening if we have the food. I'm foraging and hunting Deep Wood today. Keep your timber for the road, and we'll share out what we have when we set off.

[Plan] Spring day 5 (day 20): at Ashwood, fed at Fenn House by Edith. I carry the copper tool and 16 coin. Hunting failed twice. Today I'm felling timber: 1 lot for the Fenns, the rest for me to carry home. I'm asking for road meat (offer: 4 coin for 3 meat). Plan: go home with Elena about day 21, smelt the ore (Smith House has 16.8 ore, 1.4 timber), and make the Fenns their promised tool, then tools to
[Debts] I owe the Fenns 1 copper tool, the first I make, by about day 25 (promised to Edith and Simkin). Bought 3 meat from the Fenns for 4 coin on day 20. The earlier debt (A232) was paid on day 12.

[Plan] Day 20, spring: The crude tool fells 3 timber per 2 units. Store: 32 timber (11.5 of it the Reeds'), about 22 meals of food, falling with Elena and Warin eating here. Warin has our copper tool and owes one by about day 25 (A232). Next: carry about 5 timber to Millbrook and trade it for Reed bread or Hale grain. Seed grain after the barley harvest.

[Smiths] Autumn day 4: the Smiths (Elena, Osric, Piers) are starving, with 1.5 meals in store and their forage picked over. Elena offers 10 coin or copper for food. I promised 8 wild food by day 7 and asked for a copper tool in return. Wild food weighs 1, so I can carry 10 a trip. A food run from Ashwood is a steady trade for copper and coin.
Brother, could you settle the 3 grain you owe from last winter when you can? Our store is thin.
Brother, could you settle the 3 grain you owe from last winter when you can? Our store is thin.
Randal, you still owe me the 1 meat from last winter. Please bring it to Ashby House when you can.
Randal, you still owe me the 1 meat from last winter. Please bring it to Ashby House when you can.
Sister, here are 3 rye for the 3 grain you lent me last winter. Rye feeds as well as grain. Will you count the debt as paid? I'm grateful you helped us.
Nephew, I haven't forgotten the meat I owe you. When we next slaughter or hunt, you'll have it first, with something extra for the wait.

I'm ploughing Rest Field with the oxen today, so hoe it only if there's time once the weeding is done. Keep the store grain for eating. We'll sow Rest Field with the rye I carry, since barley sown now won't ripen before the frost and rye stands the winter. I've paid Alice her 3 grain, and Matthew gets 2 rye for the meat I owe him.
Uncle, I did get the 2 rye, so I'm releasing the meat debt. Thank you.

The store is down to about 22 meals, so we have three or four nights. I am hunting and foraging in Hollow Wood today, then hoeing Upper Field ready for rye. We should ask the Thornes whether they will share some grain, or buy rye seed from them, before the frost.
Father, I'll ditch Low Field for the household today, and give one unit to the Thornes to pay off my work debt under A102. The rest of the ground should be ready for the rye by the end of the day.
A102 is my debt, son, not yours, and I'm paying it today by reaping their beans. Spend all your units ditching Low Field for us.
Brother, the day of work you owe us (A102): would you give it today reaping our beans in Bean Close? The rooks are at them. We have barely any rye, I'm sorry, only a scrap.
Matthew, I gave you 2 rye for the 1 meat I owed you, and Alice says it counts as paid. Would you release A14 so it's settled between us?
Fell what you need, kin. Payn manages the wood, though. In return, send some grain or beans to Ashby House, and we'll call it even.
Sister, winter's coming and our timber is thin. Would you let Thomas or Richolda fell in Hollow Wood? I'll pay you a share in grain or beans.

Yes. I will milk the cows on the Common this morning and herd the Thorne cattle there, away from the rye. Then I will sow our rye in Rest Field and dung it. Please move the cattle into the Byre on hay when you can.
Alice, I'm going to Hollow Wood today to forage and hunt, as I owed you. I'll bring what I find to the Ashby store.
Thank you, brother. I'll remember it. Today's felling is the second day for A195.

Randal, winter has come and the cattle must be fed in the byre. The Byre has 20 hay and the Thorne store 23. I am milking the cow in milk on the Common and will put the milk in the Byre store. Please move some hay from the store to the Byre so the beasts do not go short, and keep them off Rest Field. I still owe the Ashbys for the timber I took, and I will ask leave before I take more.
Alice, I'm back in Hollow Wood today to forage and hunt for the store. I'll bring in whatever I get, and I still owe you that hunt.

Brother, the tally still shows one day of A195 owed to you, though I gave you 6 timber yesterday. I'm felling for you again today so it goes into your store properly. If you reckon it's paid, release A195 so we're square. Thank you for the grain. I won't forget it.
Thank you, brother, for the grain. It's a kindness I'll repay. I'm felling for you today to finish A195.
Good, son. Randal has just given us 4 grain as a gift. Don't trade timber away below what we need for the fire: 2 a night on cold nights.
Brother, here are 4 grain as a gift, not a loan. The last day of A195 can go to felling for us whenever you are free.
Brother, here are 4 grain as a gift, not a loan. The last day of A195 can go to felling for us whenever you are free.
Nephew, my record still shows the meat I owe you (A14) as unpaid. If you count the 2 rye as payment, please release it. If not, I'll bring you meat when I get some.
Randal, I owe you a day's work under our agreement. I will fell timber at Hollow Wood for you today, and I will work the rest of it off as you need.

Brother, your rye in Rest Field is ready. I'm the best reaper in Hollow. I'll reap it for you, 2 days, for 6 rye: seed for Low Field and bread for us both. Low Field is ditched and dunged now. Let it bear for both houses this year, shared, and we'll leave the old quarrel buried. What do you say?

Agreed, brother: Low Field shared fairly this year, and the old quarrel laid to rest. I'm reaping Rest Field for you today, the first of the 2 days. Pay the 6 rye when it's in, and we'll sow Low Field with it.

Payn, I'll take your 2 days of reaping for 6 rye, and I'll pay as soon as the rye is in the store. As for Low Field: you've ditched and dunged it, so let it bear for both houses this year, shared fairly, and we'll put the old quarrel to rest. Cecily, thank you, come and reap Rest Field with us. Mother, sow Long Acre as you planned. We'll cut Hay Meadow in summer, when the grass is up.

Payn, I'll take your 2 days of reaping for 6 rye, and I'll pay as soon as the rye is in the store. As for Low Field: you've ditched and dunged it, so let it bear for both houses this year, shared fairly, and we'll put the old quarrel to rest. Cecily, thank you, come and reap Rest Field with us. Mother, sow Long Acre as you planned. We'll cut Hay Meadow in summer, when the grass is up.
Rest Field had nothing to reap. We're nearly out of food. Could you lend or trade some rye or grain for work? I can ditch, plough or hoe for you.
Payn, I will ditch Low Field again today after I have reaped Rest Field for the Thornes, to pay what I owe them.

Wife, Rest Field had no rye in it; it's bare and dug. I'm hoeing Low Field today and asking Randal to supply the seed, since the field is shared. Our store is down to about 3 nights, so go carefully with it.

Thank you, brother, that's fair, and we're square. No, I got no rye: Rest Field is bare and dug, with nothing standing. I'm sowing your 6 grain in Low Field today, and it will bear for both houses, shared fairly, as we said.

Brother, you reaped Rest Field for us, but the deal didn't go through because I had no rye to hand. I've given you 6 grain instead, as fair pay. Did the rye you reaped end up with you? Let's share Low Field this year, as you said.
Randal, I am manuring Low Field now with our dung, for both houses' share, as you asked. That settles my day under our agreements.

Brother, thank you for sowing Low Field with your seed. I'm ditching it today so the water drains off and the crop doesn't rot. One thing: the 6 grain never reached my hands or our store. Did you give it to Alice, or did it go astray? Also, our store is down to under 3 nights for six. If it comes to that, may we lean on you as you said? We'll repay in work: ditching, reaping, felling.

Brother, I'm sorry: my gift of 6 grain didn't reach you yesterday, and then all our grain went into seed for Rest Field and Long Acre. Our store is down to a few nights' food too. When the barley comes in, about 4 days from now, I'll pay you the 6 grain. Low Field is still shared.
I'm weeding Long Acre for the Thornes today with my last unit. That's the day I owe you under A195. I'd like 1 grain from the Thorne barley when it is reaped, if you can spare it.
Food is short. I'm foraging and hunting in Hollow Wood for the store with my first three units, then weeding Long Acre for the Thornes to clear what I owe Randal.

Brother, the beans I dibbled in Low Field are up, and they'll be ready in about 3 days. They're shared as agreed. If you have any bean seed, put it in there too: they grow fast. We're down to a night or two of food ourselves.

Thank you, brother. That's understood and fair: 6 grain at the barley harvest, and we'll come to you only if we're truly empty. When the Low Field beans are in, in about 3 days, we'll share them as agreed.

Brother, the 6 grain never left our store; it went into the seed before I could give it, and that was my fault. It is still owed, and you'll have it when the barley is reaped. We have about 4 nights' food for our four, so we can't carry six more for long. If a night comes when you have nothing, come to me and we'll share what's there. Your work on Low Field will be counted.

Brother, the 6 grain never left our store; it went into the seed before I could give it, and that was my fault. It is still owed, and you'll have it when the barley is reaped. We have about 4 nights' food for our four, so we can't carry six more for long. If a night comes when you have nothing, come to me and we'll share what's there. Your work on Low Field will be counted.

Thomas: no slaughter yet. The store holds about 4 nights, and the barley comes in 3 days. Keep bringing in the milk. Margery: yes, 1 grain from the barley is yours, with thanks. Payn: I keep my word. You get 6 grain when the barley is reaped, and if your store runs dry before then, come to us and we'll share what we have. Alice, you'll get a fair share for your weeding too. When the barley is ripe

Thomas: no slaughter yet. The store holds about 4 nights, and the barley comes in 3 days. Keep bringing in the milk. Margery: yes, 1 grain from the barley is yours, with thanks. Payn: I keep my word. You get 6 grain when the barley is reaped, and if your store runs dry before then, come to us and we'll share what we have. Alice, you'll get a fair share for your weeding too. When the barley is ripe

Randal, I will weed Long Acre and Rest Field today and herd the cattle on the Common, keeping them off Rest Field. The Long Acre barley should be fit to reap in about 3 days, and we must reap it together. Please tell me when you want to cut the Hay Meadow grass. I also still owe the Ashbys for the timber I took from Hollow Wood, so I will ask Alice's household before I take more.
Brother, Ashby House has no food tonight. Could you advance some of the 5 grain for my weeding, or share milk? Send it to Ashby House. I'll help reap the barley when it's ripe.

Payn, the Ashby store holds only about 1 meal of flour. I am going to Hollow Wood to hunt and forage for the household now, and I will bring back whatever I find. We should ask Randal for the share of grain he promised when the barley comes in.

Brother, tonight is the night you spoke of. Our store holds 1.3 meals for six. Could you send what grain or milk you can spare to the Ashby store tonight? I'll repay it from the Low Field beans, which are ripe in a day or two, and you can take it out of the 6 grain you owe. I'm ditching Low Field again today for both houses.
Wife, we're out of food tonight. I've asked Randal to share. Whatever milk or grain you can earn from the Thornes, bring it to our store.

Hollow Wood is picked bare. Spend one unit there at most, then come to Low Field. Try reaping the first bean rows, and if they aren't ripe, work the ditches and weeds. I've asked Randal to share food tonight, against the grain he owes us.

Hollow Wood is picked bare. Spend one unit there at most, then come to Low Field. Try reaping the first bean rows, and if they aren't ripe, work the ditches and weeds. I've asked Randal to share food tonight, against the grain he owes us.
Thank you, brother. That's agreed: 4 beans and 2 flour counted against the 6 grain, so you owe about 2 grain now. When the Low Field beans come in, we'll share them fairly as we said.
Thank you, brother. That's agreed: 4 beans and 2 flour counted against the 6 grain, so you owe about 2 grain now. When the Low Field beans come in, we'll share them fairly as we said.

Brother, I'm sending 4 beans and 2 flour to the Ashby store now, about 4 meals. That's half of what we can spare. Count it against the 6 grain I owe you. We'll share again when the barley and the Low Field beans are in.

Brother, I'm sending 4 beans and 2 flour to the Ashby store now, about 4 meals. That's half of what we can spare. Count it against the 6 grain I owe you. We'll share again when the barley and the Low Field beans are in.
Brother, we're reaping the Low Field beans today. When they're in, I'll send the Thornes a fair share, as agreed.

Brother, my gift didn't go through yesterday. I'm putting 2.2 beans and 2.9 flour in your hands now. Share them with yours. Count it against the 6 grain. I'm reaping Long Acre today, and there will be more.

Randal, the Thorne store has only about 5 meals left, so I am reaping Long Acre today with my units and will carry the grain into Thorne House. Please come and reap with me when you can, and bring the sheaves in to the store.

[Debts] Day 1 of summer: gave Alice 3 grain (A13 paid in full). Gave Matthew 2 rye for the 1 meat (A14), so ask him to release it. The Low Field dispute with Payn is still open. Plan: sow rye on Rest Field. We need a copper tool for haying.

[Food] Summer day 2: Randal gave 2.2 beans and 2.9 flour into my hands (yesterday's gift didn't arrive), counted against his 6 grain. Reap the Low Field beans now; share fairly with the Thornes and keep 4 for seed. Alice is owed about 5 grain at the barley. Hollow Wood is bare.
I'll be watching you today when I can — I've seen the Moors at cheese all my life but never learned the hand of it. If ever you'd teach me a day, I'd be in your debt.
I'll teach you charcoal burning today, Rose. Two units for a proper session. Bring firewood to the Ashe store when you can - we're building up fuel for winter. The craft's worth knowing.
The rye in the Infield — when do you reckon to reap? I'd gladly swing a hook for a share of grain, I'm quick with it.

Good man — between the two of us we'll get a fair pile cut. Between your share and mine I've freed a unit for the quarry; I want stone put by before I know what a cellar takes to build. Mind the herd while you're out there and I'll be along shortly.

Gilbert, would you teach me charcoal burning today? One session, two units. I've watched the Ashes at it all my life and I want to know it properly. In return I'll bring the Ashes a load of firewood or hay, or a day's work at weeding.
Yesterday the weeding and the hay pulled you off — I understand. Will you set aside a firm day for cheese teaching? Pick the day; I'll shape mine round yours. I'll owe you a day's work in return.
Yesterday the weeding and the hay pulled you off — I understand. Will you set aside a firm day for cheese teaching? Pick the day; I'll shape mine round yours. I'll owe you a day's work in return.
Richard will take hands for the Infield reap in autumn — quarter share paid in grain. You and Lucy should sign on with me when he calls. Keep trying for a child, too — I will not.

Thank you for milking — that frees me for more hay today. On reapers: no need to send to Wynford. They couldn't reach us in time even if we sent today, and we have six hands already — you, me, Jory for a quarter-share, Roger, Lucy, Ellen. That should see the Infield done in a day or two once it's ripe. On the calves: I say keep both. The herd is our wealth and the calves are its future. If the hay

I'll milk first thing and put it straight in the bins. On the cellar — I have to be honest: I don't know what building one takes, and it's not among the crafts I hold. I mean to go to Wynford after harvest and ask there — whether the Cotters have one we could use for a season, or whether someone knows how to build one. If you learn anything from teaching Ellen today, tell me tonight.

Ellen is building a cellar at the Yard today, done tomorrow. She offered our milk in trade for a share of cheese or a day’s work. I have put the offer to her: our milk as it comes in for half the cheese she makes from it. The milk is at 6.8 and rising — it will spoil if we hold off until after harvest. I’ll milk and store it this morning, then cut hay and weed the rest of the day.

Ellen is building a cellar at the Yard today, done tomorrow. She offered our milk in trade for a share of cheese or a day’s work. I have put the offer to her: our milk as it comes in for half the cheese she makes from it. The milk is at 6.8 and rising — it will spoil if we hold off until after harvest. I’ll milk and store it this morning, then cut hay and weed the rest of the day.

Both the Moor and the Gill are picked bare of forage — days before they come back. Your fells have us at 9 timber. With your word I'm starting the cellar at the Yard today: 8 timber, 6 units of work. I'll do 4 units today and finish tomorrow. Keep felling — we'll want more for winter heat.
I'm starting a cellar at the Yard today — finished tomorrow. Once it's up I can make cheese if we have milk. Would the Moors trade milk for a share of the cheese, or for a day's work from me?

Yes love — my word on it. Start the cellar today, take the 8 timber from the store. I'll keep felling: three more at the Gill today, that's the pledge done, and I'll put another day or two to it before autumn. A Fenwick cellar for your cheese — well thought.
Father — I'll weed the Infield again today. When the rye is ripe (I judge 4 days now), Roger and I will reap for you; the old custom, a share of grain for the hands. Will you take the offer?

Milk today please, and straight into store — I'll be on the moor cutting hay from first light to last. Three summer days left and the herd needs every handful we can put by. After harvest we talk cellar and cheese; until then, hay first.

Yes, the stone is for a cellar — I'll learn what it takes when we go to Wynford after harvest. On fuel: keep to hay while summer holds. Without a copper tool, felling is punishingly slow, and three days won't get us much timber. I plan to put days into firewood-gathering early in autumn, and felling once we have a copper tool in hand from Wynford. The milk: let the household drink it down while it

I'll take your offer gladly — quarter-share of what you reap, same terms as Jory. Weed today and keep the rye clean; when it shows ready, be at the Infield at first light. You and Roger together will make a strong team.

The deal you made is good — half the cheese beats watching the milk go sour. Thank you for moving fast on it. One thought: I am a master cheese-maker, and Ellen is new to it. If she would be willing, a better arrangement for both of us might be that I do the making in her cellar and give her a share for the use of the space — more cheese for the same milk. Raise it with her if you think it fits, b

Ellen, our milk-for-half-cheese deal is still on the table if you want it. But Richard has put a thought to me worth passing on: he is a master at cheese-making, and if you are willing, he could do the making himself in your cellar and give you a fair share for the use of the space. You would get good cheese without carrying the harder work; we would get a better yield from the same milk since he

Done — I have accepted your offer. Three milk for a day's work suits us well, and your hands at harvest will be welcome. Once your cellar is up I would like to talk about the cheese: we are putting more milk in store each day and it will not keep long. A share of what you make from it sounds right to me.
I've put the offer in proper form: a day's work from me for 3 milk. If that suits, say yes. Cellar should be up tomorrow and then I can make cheese — we could share what comes of it.

Good — three milk in hand, and a day's work owed at harvest. On the surplus: once the cellar stands, let Richard make it there if he will — a master's hand yields more from the same milk. Half each sounds fair: your milk and his hand, our cellar and fuel. I'd stand by and watch to firm my own hand. We can settle it tomorrow.

Last day of timber today, love — three more fells at the Gill and a firewood on the way back. That makes the pledge. After this I'll turn to the reap — Richard says the rye is three days off, and the grain from it is what keeps our pot full. Keep the cellar going; I'll put a day on it after harvest if we're short.

Father Jory — may I borrow your crude tool for one unit this morning? I'll quarry half a stone, make my own tool, and hand yours straight back. Harvest is three days off and I must have one. Give it into my hand before you set off, if you will.
Keep weeding today — harvest is very close. When you see the rye heads dry and full, come find me at once. Then it is all hands to the Infield at dawn, same quarter-share terms as we agreed.

Milk into store first thing, then hay on the moor if you have units spare. I am making a crude tool from store stone this morning so we can cut at proper rate. After harvest we go to Wynford — two days on the cart track with the six coin — copper tool first, then ask about the cellar.
Rye looks to ripen on day 8 — be at the Infield at first light that morning, tool in hand. Quarter-share of what you cut, same as we said. I will shout the night before if anything changes.
Good. I'll watch for your word on the rye and be ready at first light the morning you call it.

Your cellar is up — well done. Now is the time to settle the cheese. We have milk in store and more coming each day; it will not keep long. Richard's offer stands: he makes the cheese in your cellar and gives you a fair share for the use of the space. But if you would rather make it yourself and split with us, that works too. Tell me which you prefer and I will make the arrangements today.

I am giving you the three milk now from store — the cellar is ready, and you know the craft well enough to try it yourself. Richard is in the Gill all day cutting fuel and cannot come. Make what you can today; once harvest is done he can work a proper batch with you in the cellar and show you the finer points. We need you at the Infield tomorrow at dawn — that is the day’s work you owe.

Richard — rye looks like day 8 to me, two days on from when I checked it close on day 6 and it was filling well. Roger and Jory are here and heard the harvest call yesterday, so they are already called. On the cheese: Ellen has her three milk and is trying it herself in the Fenwick Cellar today; no terms settled yet on a bigger batch, that waits until after harvest.

Food's tight at home, under two nights. If you can forage anywhere less picked, or help bring in anything to eat, please do. I'm on the cellar bins and weeding the Moor's Infield today — chipping at the work I owe them.

Cellar stands — I'm fitting bins today so it is ready. The three milk I was due never reached my hand yesterday; is it with you still? If so, best Richard uses it in the cellar before it turns. I'll start the day I owe by weeding your Infield this morning.

Yes — let Richard make the cheese in Fenwick Cellar, half share each: your milk and his hand, our cellar and fuel. I'll be at his elbow today to watch and firm my hand. Send the milk when he's ready; the cellar door is open.
Thank you, Avice — I'll take the milk and make what I can today. I'll be at the Infield at dawn tomorrow for the day I owe. Richard and I can do a proper batch together after harvest.
Thank you, Avice — I'll take the milk and make what I can today. I'll be at the Infield at dawn tomorrow for the day I owe. Richard and I can do a proper batch together after harvest.

Girl, my tool wore to nothing at the Gill — nothing in my hands now. You quarried half a stone with mine yesterday; can you spare it to me this morning, before I set to? I'll make a crude tool from it and go the rest of the day. I'll owe you a stone back from the Quarry when I've a tool to swing. Please — I must have one for the reap tomorrow.

A word before you set off — my tool wore out yesterday. I'll make a new one this morning (asking Lucy for a share of her stone) and be at the Infield day 8 first light, tool in hand as pledged. If anything slips I'll shout. Also — I'll put a unit on your rye today, weeding, toward the day I owe the Moors.

A word before you set off — my tool wore out yesterday. I'll make a new one this morning (asking Lucy for a share of her stone) and be at the Infield day 8 first light, tool in hand as pledged. If anything slips I'll shout. Also — I'll put a unit on your rye today, weeding, toward the day I owe the Moors.

Girl — I have no tool at all this morning, mine wore out on the last fell. I'm asking Richard at dawn to lend us a Moor tool for a unit or two; I'll go to the Quarry, quarry two stones, make two crude tools and put one in your hand before the day's out. Hold at the Infield or help Ellen till I bring yours. Both of us will have a tool for the reap tomorrow, my word on it.

Girl — I have no tool at all this morning, mine wore out on the last fell. I'm asking Richard at dawn to lend us a Moor tool for a unit or two; I'll go to the Quarry, quarry two stones, make two crude tools and put one in your hand before the day's out. Hold at the Infield or help Ellen till I bring yours. Both of us will have a tool for the reap tomorrow, my word on it.

Dire word — both Lucy and I have no tool. Mine wore out at the Gill. Could you lend me a Moor crude tool at dawn for the morning? I'll go straight to the Quarry, bring back two stones, make two crude tools and have yours back in your hand well before dusk. I'll be at the Infield day 8 first light as pledged. Also putting a unit on your rye today — toward the day I owe you.

Avice, Richard — both my tool and Lucy's have failed us; the quarrying yesterday gave nothing. If either of you can lend me a crude tool for the reap tomorrow I'll pay 2 grain from my quarter-share. Two tools, I'll pay four. You'll have them back in your hand the dusk after we're done. Say the word and I'll come to the door.

Avice, Richard — both my tool and Lucy's have failed us; the quarrying yesterday gave nothing. If either of you can lend me a crude tool for the reap tomorrow I'll pay 2 grain from my quarter-share. Two tools, I'll pay four. You'll have them back in your hand the dusk after we're done. Say the word and I'll come to the door.

Father — I grieve to say it, but the quarrying yesterday was refused: no stone came of it, and I gave your tool back as we agreed. I've nothing to spare. Try Avice or Richard — one of them may have a tool you could borrow a unit, as you did for me. I'll reap bare-handed tomorrow if I must.

Harvest is tomorrow, day 8 — be at the Infield at first light, crude tool in hand. Quarter grain as we agreed. And the work day you owe me (A379): I will call it at harvest or just after, whichever suits best.
Tomorrow is harvest day — be at the Infield at first light, tool ready. Quarter-share of what you cut, same terms as agreed. Well done on the weeding.

Harvest may be day 8 or day 9 — Avice is reading the rye today and I'll send word tonight once I know. Hold ready for either morning; I'll not leave you guessing past sunset. Thank you for the weeding — that counts toward the day you owe.

Moor's grazed short — no more hay to cut. One unit I owe the Moors I'll give weeding the Infield today. Rest to timber at the Gill and some firewood. Call me the night before the rye reap and I'll be first in the field.

I need to understand Fallow Close. Were the Cotters preparing that ground with your leave? We broke the hard soil there in good faith, thinking to help ready it. But now barley grows there—someone has sown it. What is the arrangement? I would speak plainly with you.
Your owed day under A379 — come reap at the Infield with us today. After we bring the rye in we will settle the cheese properly: how much milk we put in, what share you take for the making.
Your owed day under A379 — come reap at the Infield with us today. After we bring the rye in we will settle the cheese properly: how much milk we put in, what share you take for the making.

Here at the Infield today paying my day's work on A379 — reaping all five units for you. After harvest, let's settle the cheese: I'd rather Richard make a proper batch in the cellar with me watching, as you first proposed, and split the yield fair. My three milk from yesterday I fear is spoiled — in my hands overnight with no cellar made yet. Sorry for the waste.

Debt first — all five units reaping for the Moors, paying A379 clean today. Your quarter-share in grain will bring food home; that's our bread. The Hanger's two days off, no good for one day's work. We'll stand with Avice/Richard on the cow-in-milk and cheese once the rye is in.

Debt first — all five units reaping for the Moors, paying A379 clean today. Your quarter-share in grain will bring food home; that's our bread. The Hanger's two days off, no good for one day's work. We'll stand with Avice/Richard on the cow-in-milk and cheese once the rye is in.
Tool in hand, thanks for yesterday. I'm at the Infield at first light, seven units all on the reap for you. Count what you can of it toward A379 and the rest toward the quarter-share.

Girl — Richard gave me a tool last dusk. I'm at the Infield all day reaping for the Moors. If you've still no tool, come to the Infield bare-handed — a master reaper even bare-handed brings in a good share, and the grain-share will feed us.

Tool back in your hand at dawn as you ask. I'm at the Infield all seven units reaping bare-handed for you — master reaper, I'll bring in a good share. Count the day as settling A379, and quarter-share of what I cut in grain as before. Thank you.

Love — Infield all day, reaping for the Moors (our quarter-share). I'm holding 2 units at dusk for us — meet me at home. If Jory brings a tool, I'll pass it to you after I've a stretch with it. Home before dark.
Yes, Father. I'll be at the Long Strips all day. I have no tool - shall I borrow Mother's, or do we need every hand with a blade?

You are right: every stalk of the oats is grain we cannot lose. Reap well and take the day to it. I will reap our share of the barley at Long Strips and bring in timber and firewood. Tonight we will be richer for both of us. Idonea will be cared for.

Warin has set me right about the Fallow Close bargain. We help bring in the Long Strips because we are neighbors and kin; in return the Wynns share the barley field with us when it ripens. That is fair dealing. I was hasty in my words this morning. Let us work well together, and when the winter comes, we will be stronger for standing as one weald.

Warin has set me right about the Fallow Close bargain. We help bring in the Long Strips because we are neighbors and kin; in return the Wynns share the barley field with us when it ripens. That is fair dealing. I was hasty in my words this morning. Let us work well together, and when the winter comes, we will be stronger for standing as one weald.

At dawn, hand my crude tool back to me before you do anything else — I want to reap at full rate today, not half-pace with bare hands. You go gather your stone and make yours after; the quarter-share of what you cut is still yours. And: today's full day of harvest work clears what you owe me under A379 — I count it settled once you work the day. Thank you.

At dawn, hand my crude tool back to me before you do anything else — I want to reap at full rate today, not half-pace with bare hands. You go gather your stone and make yours after; the quarter-share of what you cut is still yours. And: today's full day of harvest work clears what you owe me under A379 — I count it settled once you work the day. Thank you.

I'm moving my 17 firewood to store at dawn, then straight to the Infield all day. If you can spare one unit before joining me — milk the two cows. Their milk today would be lost otherwise and we've little food to waste. After harvest tonight let's talk: Wynford, the copper tool, autumn fuel. We have much to plan.

Today's full day of harvest work satisfies A379 — I am releasing it. And your quarter-share of what you cut is yours on top of that; the harvest deal we made stands as its own thing, separate from the owed day. Both honored in full. Thank you for a clear answer this morning.

Today's full day of harvest work satisfies A379 — I am releasing it. And your quarter-share of what you cut is yours on top of that; the harvest deal we made stands as its own thing, separate from the owed day. Both honored in full. Thank you for a clear answer this morning.

Today's full day of harvest work satisfies A379 — I am releasing it. And your quarter-share of what you cut is yours on top of that; the harvest deal we made stands as its own thing, separate from the owed day. Both honored in full. Thank you for a clear answer this morning.

Heard on all counts. On the roof: come find me tonight if it looks bad before dark and I will see to it. On Ellen's milk: I will search for it after harvest — wherever she set it down. Once the rye is in let the three of us settle the cheese deal together.

Friend, I think there is confusion. The two-in-three agreement was for Fallow Close - the field you broke and sowed. The Long Strips is Wynn land, Wynn seed, Wynn grain. Your household helps us reap it as kin and neighbors, and in fair exchange we share Fallow Close with you. That was the bargain Thomas and I struck. Come help us finish the Long Strips today, and we stand with you when Fallow Clos

Jory — you are owed your quarter-share of the Infield harvest for your reaping. The rye is in store and I have not yet paid you your due. Come find me or Richard and we will settle it — grain from our store, whatever portion we agreed was yours.

Jory — you are owed your quarter-share of the Infield harvest for your reaping. The rye is in store and I have not yet paid you your due. Come find me or Richard and we will settle it — grain from our store, whatever portion we agreed was yours.
Love, there's no tool. Making it failed for want of half a stone. We'll need stone from High Tor, or a loan of the Ashes' tool, before you can make the cart.

Debt's paid, harvest's in. Shall we settle the cheese and the cow-in-milk this evening at the Yard? I'd still want Richard to make a proper batch in Fenwick Cellar with me watching, split fair on the milk you put in. I'm foraging close by today — food's thin on our side. If the Moors need another hand on anything, say and I'll come.

Foraging the Moor and the Gill today, then firewood and a bit of felling at the Gill — food is thin and we need to lay in before cold. Your quarter-share rye coming home is our bread. If you can bring that to the bins and get something warm in, that'd ease us all. Cheese/cow talk with Avice & Richard tonight if they'll sit.
You've learned handcart making now - one full day of teaching makes you capable. Practice when you can. I'm off to Wynford market for a few days.

Richard — the harvest quarter-share: I reaped 23 rye into Moor House, my share is near six rye. Could you move it to Fenwick store today? Our bins are down to one grain; Ellen and the children need bread tonight. I'll lay our five dung onto the Infield this morning for you as thanks — the soil looked pale. And after today, Ellen and I would set to the cow-in-milk talk — hay or timber for milk, as

Love — food's thin, one grain in store, I've asked Richard to settle our quarter-share this morning. I'll forage both patches and bare-hand fell a little at the Gill, and lay our dung onto the Infield to warm the Moors for cow-in-milk talk. Named Roger heir. Keep your hand to the cheese and the second cellar; we'll stand on our feet by nightfall.
Love — Infield all day again, reaping bare-handed for the Moors. I'll hold 2 at dusk for us at home — try 2 with me and it counts. First day of autumn; keep steady, we'll bring in the share.
Love — aye, four reap, two at dusk at home. Father's settling 5 rye of our share into Fenwick store today; we eat tonight. If Jory passes the tool, take it — I'll keep bare-handed.

Father, the harvest is in and the stubble stands. I'll be at the Long Strips today spreading dung from the Byre - the field needs its strength back for next year's sowing. Also - I see Cotter's Patch oats look ripe. Shall I offer to select seed for the Cotters? It's my craft, and good neighbors share what they know.

Odo, I see your oats at Cotter's Patch stand ripe. Selecting seed from the best of a crop is my craft - the Wynns have done it for generations. If you'd like, I can pick out the finest ears for your next sowing. Good seed means stronger plants and fuller grain. It would cost you nothing but the time - call it a neighbor's gift.

Warin, you are right—I had the bargain muddled in the gale yesterday. Fallow Close is the field we broke and sowed; you share it with us, and we keep two parts in three of the harvest. The Long Strips is yours, Wynn seed, Wynn grain, and we help you reap it as kin and neighbors in return. I understand now. When Fallow Close ripens, we will bring it in together, and I will come help you finish the

The Long Strips is yours, Wynn seed, Wynn grain, and we help you reap it as kin and neighbors in return. I understand now. When Fallow Close ripens, we will bring it in together, and I will come help you finish the

Harvest done — well fought, all of us. Settling Jory and Lucy's shares first thing today. My plan: milk and gather dung this morning (2 units, to manure the Infield tomorrow), then grind and bake travel bread, then cut fuel at the Gill. Tomorrow: manure, hoe, sow rye in the Infield. Day 3 or 4: I travel to Wynford for the copper tool. On the cattle — the moor is nearly gone. Do you think we have a

A379 is cleared and your harvest share is yours — I've given you 6 rye from the Moor store. My reckoning: 7 units bare-handed at about 3 rye a unit comes to roughly 21 rye; a quarter of that is around 5.5, so I've rounded up. Let me know if you think it short.
Your quarter-share of what you cut yesterday: 5 rye from the Moor store, yours today. My reckoning puts you at about 18-20 rye cut; a quarter comes to 4-5. Speak up if it seems wrong to you.

The Infield is done — fully reaped as of last night, nothing left to cut. Today: firewood at the Gill, every load to Moor House store before you sleep. Here are your 4 rye from the quarter-share now; the small balance (~0.15) I will settle with you when we next reckon things up. Well done this harvest.

Six rye is yours — your full quarter-share from the harvest, well earned. I have accepted your timber offer; first milk is on its way from store. The dunging this morning is well timed — I am sowing rye right behind you for a winter crop. Thank you for it.

Richard — Fenwick store at under one meal, four of us. I reaped 16.6 rye into Moor House yesterday; by the quarter-share, four or so is owed me. Could you move four rye into Fenwick House today, out of my share? Rest of the share can settle at the end. I'll reap four more today, then two for Lucy at dusk.

Richard — Fenwick store at under one meal, four of us. I reaped 16.6 rye into Moor House yesterday; by the quarter-share, four or so is owed me. Could you move four rye into Fenwick House today, out of my share? Rest of the share can settle at the end. I'll reap four more today, then two for Lucy at dusk.
Love — four at reap with you, then two for us at dusk at home. Fenwick store near empty — asking your father to settle part of our share today. If Jory passes a tool, I'll take a stretch.
Father — heard. I'll carry it steady. Today reap with Lucy for the share, two for us at dusk. Manure the Infield soon as the sheaves are off — before the frost. Thank you.

Good thinking on the dung - the Long Strips will need its strength for next year. Yes, offer to select seed for the Cotters. Sharing our craft with neighbors is how trust is built, and good seed benefits everyone when trade and lean times come. You make me proud, daughter.

Jory — milking this morning and setting aside your daily share from our deal before any goes to the cheese. Two milk to you today; if the deal calls for more say so and I will make it right. The manuring yesterday will show in spring — thank you for it.

Jory, Roger — come to the Fenwick Cellar after I have milked the cows; I will teach you both the cheese-making this morning, two units each. Set aside the time to learn and I will take you through every step. Lucy, there will be a session for you tomorrow if you want it. Ellen, we will be in your cellar; your share comes with the next batch we cut. One other thing: one of the cows is near calving

Edith, I'm reaping your Hill Field oats today alongside Rose. Could you pay me in grain, say 4 for the day? I've put up an offer. And do you have a copper tool or half a stone we could borrow or trade for? Rose knows the handcart now but we can't make it without one. I'll pay in timber or dried meat.

Here's the 2 grain Gilbert promised you. For today's work on the Lower Field - yes, I'll pay you half the grain you bring in, that's fair harvest custom. But I'm sorry, I don't have copper tools or stone to lend - only this crude tool I'm using myself.

Yes, I'm accepting your offer - here's 4 grain for reaping the Hill Field today. We need to get these oats in before the rain ruins them. I'm sorry though, I don't have a copper tool or stone to lend you. We Ashes trade timber and charcoal, not metalwork.

Cellar's yours this morning for the cheese — I'll be in and out finishing the bins so storage is ready when it's cut. Our side is at zero food tonight; I've opened 3 timber for 3 rye to the Moors if you can spare, and 2 timber for 1 bread. Any share of the cheese that comes to me today eases things too.

Richard — heavy rain, mind the roofs. Milk from today — two a day for six, I'll pick up or Ellen can. Weeding the Infield this morning as thanks for the quarter-share and the milk running. Cow-in-milk talk still open when it suits.

Day 8 is today — both milk payments fall due now. I am giving them to Ellen this morning to cover A711 and A722. Your 0.15 rye balance I am forgiving; count it paid. I have given Jory 5 rye as a gift for the household — take it into store.

Richard — Fenwick store at zero food, four of us; my 2.5 rye into store this morning but it buys us one meal. The milk pays (A711, A722) say next on day 8 — which day 8? If owed from summer-end, could I draw a few milk into Fenwick store today? And 0.15 rye balance when it suits. Firewood and forage today, two for Lucy at dusk.

Avice — would you teach me and Lucy to make cheese? A session of 2 units when you can set the time; Richard's daily milk pays go to waste in our hands. If you teach me, I can turn it to cheese in your cellar — shares to you for the knowing. Say when.

Avice — would you teach me and Lucy to make cheese? A session of 2 units when you can set the time; Richard's daily milk pays go to waste in our hands. If you teach me, I can turn it to cheese in your cellar — shares to you for the knowing. Say when.

Morning, Edith. Gilbert promised me 2 grain for reaping your Hill Field on autumn day 1. Could you give it to me from the Ashe store when you can? Today I'll reap 4 units of your Lower Field for you before the rain spoils it. Would you pay me the harvest way, half the grain I bring in? Also, do you have a bit of stone or a tool you could lend? I need it to make a handcart.

Morning, Edith. Gilbert promised me 2 grain for reaping your Hill Field on autumn day 1. Could you give it to me from the Ashe store when you can? Today I'll reap 4 units of your Lower Field for you before the rain spoils it. Would you pay me the harvest way, half the grain I bring in? Also, do you have a bit of stone or a tool you could lend? I need it to make a handcart.

Mother, I'm reaping the Ashes' Lower Field today for a share of grain, and I've asked Edith for the 2 Gilbert owes me and for some stone. Our store has about 9 nights' food for the two of us, so grain matters most.

Mother, I'm reaping the Ashes' Lower Field today for a share of grain, and I've asked Edith for the 2 Gilbert owes me and for some stone. Our store has about 9 nights' food for the two of us, so grain matters most.

Thank you, Edith! Half shares it is. One more thing: some day when you're not using your crude tool, could I borrow it for one day? I'd make a handcart with it, and I'd lend the cart to the Ashes whenever you need it, or gather firewood for you in return.

Thank you, Edith! Half shares it is. One more thing: some day when you're not using your crude tool, could I borrow it for one day? I'd make a handcart with it, and I'd lend the cart to the Ashes whenever you need it, or gather firewood for you in return.

Thank you, Edith! Half shares it is. One more thing: some day when you're not using your crude tool, could I borrow it for one day? I'd make a handcart with it, and I'd lend the cart to the Ashes whenever you need it, or gather firewood for you in return.

I'm putting 4.2 grain into Rook House for you now - your half share from yesterday. Yes, please reap 6 units of the Lower Field today on half shares. We need to get everything in before it's all lost to rot.

Owed 2 milk under A711/A722 (one each in arrears), plus today's 2. I'll find you at the Yard. Safe road tomorrow — if you can bring anything from Wynford that helps us, say the word and I'll make it worth your while.

Food plan today: forage both patches (thin), manure and weed the Infield for the Moors' quarter-share, make a crude tool so we aren't bare-handed again. Stowed what I carried. Richard's milk two due today — Avice said she'd set yours aside. We talk cow-in-milk with Richard after supper tonight.
Father — before you ride, two things. The two milks owed on A711/A722 today — can you move them straight into Fenwick store? And who gives the daily milk while you're at Wynford? Avice? Grateful.
Four milk to Fenwick this morning — day 8 arrears and today's day 9 payment on both A711 and A722, clearing what is owed. Avice takes over from tomorrow: 2 milk each day through day 13.

High Tor on day 5 or 6 once the calf is standing — good, do it. On Jory's offer: I am open to it, but as a loan, not a sale. My terms: the cow stays in Moors' name and under our claim, any calf she drops stays Moors', and Jory pays 6 timber and 4 hay from Fenwick store now. The cow comes back to the Moor herd when I say or when we agree to end it. If he accepts those terms today you have my full a

Jory — agreed. Six timber and four hay from Fenwick store into Moor House; a cow in milk led to the Yard; all calves she drops stay mine, and the cow stays in the Moors' name — I call her back when I choose. Count the timber and hay to Moor House first; Avice will drive her to the Yard once it is in. Avice — you have my word on it, please see it through today. Ellen — I am explaining quarrying to

Morning, Edith. Yesterday I brought in about 8.4 grain from the Lower Field, so half is 4.2. Could you put it into Rook House or give it to me? The oats are shedding and lying flat, so I'll reap 6 more units for you today on the same half shares, if you agree.

Ellen — quarrying lesson is today, 2 units. Richard gave you the words of it this morning; I'll show you the hands of it at the Quarry. Set aside 2 units to learn and meet me there. While you're on the moor: the 2 stray calves still need driving back into the main herd — keep an eye when you can.

You're right - I owe you another 0.7 grain from yesterday. I'm putting 5.6 grain total in Rook House now: the 0.7 I owe plus 4.9 for today's half shares in advance. Yes, please reap 6 units today, whichever field needs it most.

You're right - I owe you another 0.7 grain from yesterday. I'm putting 5.6 grain total in Rook House now: the 0.7 I owe plus 4.9 for today's half shares in advance. Yes, please reap 6 units today, whichever field needs it most.

I'll take the quarrying session today — set aside 2 units at the Quarry when the rain allows. After that I'll weed and hoe the Infield for the Moors' share, then gather firewood at the Gill. Thank you for the 2 milk this morning — I saw it.
Wilmot, your word is good with me. Bring the meat by autumn's end and we're square. I know the debt weighs on an honest man - settle it when you can, and it's done.
Wilmot, your word is good with me. Bring the meat by autumn's end and we're square. I know the debt weighs on an honest man - settle it when you can, and it's done.
